chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 1 — Padua. A public place
paragraphs: Flourish. Enter Lucentio and Tranio.

LUCENTIO. Tranio, because of my great desire to see fair Padua, the nursery of the arts, I have arrived in fruitful Lombardy, the pleasant garden of great Italy. With my father's love and permission, I'm armed with his good will and your trusted company — you, my reliable servant, proven in everything. Let's catch our breath here and, with luck, begin a course of learning and serious studies. Pisa, famous for its respected citizens, gave me my birth, and my father before me — Vincentio, a great international merchant, descended from the Bentivolii. Vincentio's son, raised in Florence, should live up to every hope placed in him, decorating his family's fortune with virtuous deeds. So, Tranio, while I'm studying, I'll devote myself to virtue and to that branch of philosophy that deals with happiness — happiness achieved specifically through virtue. Tell me what you think. I've left Pisa and come to Padua like someone abandoning a shallow puddle to plunge into the deep, seeking to quench his thirst by drinking his fill.

TRANIO. _Mi perdonato_, my gentle master. I feel exactly as you do — glad you're sticking to your plan to drink in the sweetness of philosophy. Only, good master, while we admire this virtue and moral discipline, let's not become stoics or stones, please. And don't be so devoted to Aristotle's restraints that you completely reject Ovid. Practise logic with friends, and use rhetoric in everyday conversation. Use music and poetry to keep yourself alive. Tackle mathematics and metaphysics whenever you have the stomach for them. No profit comes from anything without pleasure. In short, sir, study what you most enjoy.

LUCENTIO. Thanks, Tranio — that's good advice. If Biondello had come ashore, we could get ourselves settled right away and find lodgings suitable to entertain whatever friends time brings us in Padua. But wait a moment — who are these people?
TRANIO. Master, some sort of show to welcome us to town.
[_Lucentio and Tranio stand aside._]
Enter Baptista, Katherina, Bianca, Gremio and Hortensio.

BAPTISTA. Gentlemen, don't press me any further. You know I'm firmly decided: I will not give my younger daughter away before I've found a husband for the elder. If either of you loves Katherina — and because I know you both well and like you both — you have my permission to court her as you please.
GREMIO. Cart her, more like — she's too rough for me. There, Hortensio, do you want a wife?
KATHERINA.
[_To Baptista_] I beg you, sir, is it your wish
to make a laughingstock of me in front of these men?
HORTENSIO. Men, girl! What do you mean by that? No man for you, unless you were of gentler, milder stuff.

KATHERINA. Honestly, sir, you'll never need to worry. I assure you, marriage isn't halfway to my heart. But if it were, you can be sure my concern would be to comb your skull with a three-legged stool, paint your face, and treat you like a fool.
HORTENSIO. From all such devils, good Lord deliver us!
GREMIO. And me too, good Lord!
TRANIO. Quiet, master! There's some good entertainment coming. That girl is either stark mad or remarkably willful.
LUCENTIO. But in the silence of the other one, I see a girl's mild manners and modesty. Quiet, Tranio!
TRANIO. Well said, master — hush! And look your fill.
BAPTISTA. Gentlemen, so I can quickly make good on what I've said — Bianca, go inside. And don't let this upset you, sweet Bianca. I'll love you no less for it, my girl.
KATHERINA. A precious pet! She should stick her finger in her eye and cry, if she knew why.
BIANCA. Sister, find your contentment in my discontent. Sir, I humbly submit to your wishes. My books and instruments will be my companions — I'll look at them, and practise by myself.
LUCENTIO. Listen, Tranio! You may hear Minerva herself speaking.
HORTENSIO. Signior Baptista, will you really be so distant? I'm sorry our good intentions cause Bianca grief.
GREMIO. Why would you lock her up, Signior Baptista, on account of this hellish fiend, and make her pay the price of her sister's tongue?
BAPTISTA. Gentlemen, settle down — I've made up my mind. Go inside, Bianca.
[_Exit Bianca._]

And since I know she takes the greatest delight in music, instruments, and poetry, I'll keep schoolmasters in my house qualified to instruct her youth. If you, Hortensio, or you, Signior Gremio, know any such men, send them to me. I'll be very kind to skilled men, and generous toward giving my own children a good upbringing. So, farewell. Katherina, you can stay — I have more to discuss with Bianca.
[_Exit._]
KATHERINA. Why, and I trust I'm free to leave too, am I not? What — am I to have my hours assigned, as if, presumably, I didn't know what to do and what not to do? Ha!
[_Exit._]

GREMIO. You can go to the devil's mother — your gifts are so wonderful that nobody here is going to hold you back. Their love isn't so strong, Hortensio, that we can't blow on our fingers together and wait it out. Our cake is dough on both sides. Farewell — though, for the love I have for my sweet Bianca, if I can by any means find a suitable man to teach her what she likes, I'll recommend him to her father.

HORTENSIO. So will I, Signior Gremio. But a word, please. Though our rivalry has never let us talk before, now, after some thought, it concerns us both — that is, so we may again have access to our lovely lady and be happy rivals for Bianca's love — we ought to work together on one specific thing.
GREMIO. What's that, pray?
HORTENSIO. To get a husband for her sister, of course.
GREMIO. A husband! You mean a devil.
HORTENSIO. I said a husband.
GREMIO. I said a devil. Do you really think, Hortensio, that even though her father is rich, any man is fool enough to marry hell?

HORTENSIO. Come on, Gremio! Though it goes beyond your patience and mine to put up with her loud outbursts, there are good fellows in the world, man — and if a man could find them, they would take her with all her faults, provided there's enough money.
GREMIO. I can't say. But I'd just as soon take her dowry on this condition: that I be whipped at the public cross every morning.

HORTENSIO. As you say — there's small choice among rotten apples. But come on. Since this legal obstacle has made us friends, let's keep it friendly to that extent — until, by helping Baptista's eldest daughter to a husband, we set his youngest free to be married — and then we go at it again. Sweet Bianca! May the best man win! The one who runs fastest gets the prize. What do you say, Signior Gremio?
GREMIO. Agreed. I'd give the best horse in Padua to the man who'd court her thoroughly, marry her, bed her, and rid the house of her. Let's go.
[_Exeunt Gremio and Hortensio._]
TRANIO. I beg you, sir, tell me — is it really possible that love should take such a sudden hold?

LUCENTIO. Oh Tranio! Until I felt it myself, I never thought it possible or even likely. But look — while I stood idly watching, I felt the effect of love-in-idleness. And now I admit plainly to you, who are as private and as dear to me as Anna was to the Queen of Carthage — Tranio, I burn, I pine, I am dying, Tranio, if I don't have this young modest girl. Counsel me, Tranio, because I know you can. Help me, Tranio, because I know you will.
TRANIO. Master, it's no time to scold you now. Affection isn't reasoned out of the heart. If love has struck you, nothing remains but this: _Redime te captum quam queas minimo._
LUCENTIO. Thanks, lad — go on. That helps. The rest will comfort me, because your advice is sound.
TRANIO. Master, you looked so long at the girl, you may not have caught the essential point.
LUCENTIO. Oh, yes — I saw sweet beauty in her face, like the beauty of Agenor's daughter, the one that made great Jove kneel and kiss the Cretan shore.
TRANIO. Did you see no more? Did you not notice how her sister began to scold and raise such a storm that mortal ears could barely stand the racket?
LUCENTIO. Tranio, I saw her coral lips moving, and her breath perfumed the air. Everything I saw of her was sacred and sweet.

TRANIO. All right, then — it's time to shake him out of his trance. Please wake up, sir. If you love the girl, bend your thoughts and your wits to winning her. Here's how things stand: her elder sister is so vicious and shrewish that until her father gets her off his hands, master, your love will have to live as a maid at home. He has shut her up tight on purpose, because he doesn't want suitors bothering her.
LUCENTIO. Ah, Tranio, what a cruel father! But haven't you heard he took some trouble to find skilled schoolmasters to instruct her?
TRANIO. Yes, indeed I have, sir — and now the scheme is taking shape.
LUCENTIO. I've got it, Tranio.
TRANIO. Master, I'd bet my hand both our ideas meet and fit as one.
LUCENTIO. Tell me yours first.
TRANIO. You'll become the schoolmaster, and take on the teaching of the girl. That's your plan.
LUCENTIO. It is — but can it be done?
TRANIO. Impossible — because who's going to play your part and be Vincentio's son here in Padua? Who keeps house and studies, welcomes friends, visits countrymen, and entertains them?

LUCENTIO. _Basta_, calm down — I've thought it through. We haven't been seen at any house yet, and no one can tell our faces apart for master and man. So it follows: you'll be master in my place, Tranio. Keep up the house and rank and servants, as I should. I'll be someone else — some Florentine, some Neapolitan, or some lesser man from Pisa. It's hatched, and so it shall be. Tranio, undress at once — take my coloured hat and cloak. When Biondello arrives, he'll wait on you. But I'll first convince him to keep his tongue quiet.
[_They exchange habits._]

TRANIO. You'd better. In short, sir, since this is what you want, and I'm bound to obey — for so your father instructed me at our parting: 'Be helpful to my son,' he said, although I think he meant it in another sense — I'm content to be Lucentio, because I love Lucentio so well.
LUCENTIO. Tranio, be so, because Lucentio loves. And let me be a slave, if it means winning the girl whose sudden sight has captured my wounded eye.
Enter Biondello.
Here comes the rogue. Hey, where have you been?
BIONDELLO. Where have I been? No — how about this: where are you? Master, has my fellow Tranio stolen your clothes? Or have you stolen his? Or both? Tell me, what's the news?

LUCENTIO. Hey, come here. This is no time for jokes — so adjust your manners to the situation. Your fellow Tranio here, to save my life, has put on my clothes and my appearance, and I, to escape, have put on his. In a fight since I came ashore I killed a man, and I'm afraid I was spotted. Wait on him, I order you, as you should — while I get out of here to save my life. Do you understand me?
BIONDELLO. I, sir! Not at all.
LUCENTIO. And not a word of Tranio out of your mouth. Tranio is changed into Lucentio.
BIONDELLO. Lucky him — I wish I could swap too!

TRANIO. So could I, boy — for the next wish in line, that Lucentio really did get Baptista's youngest daughter. But, fellow, not for my sake but your master's, I'm advising you: use your manners carefully in every kind of company. When I'm alone, I'm Tranio; but in all other places, your master Lucentio.
LUCENTIO. Tranio, let's go. One more thing remains for you to do — to join up with these suitors. If you ask me why, it's enough that my reasons are good and weighty.
[_Exeunt._]
[_The Presenters above speak._]
FIRST SERVANT. My lord, you're nodding off — you're not paying attention to the play.
SLY. Yes I am, by Saint Anne. A good story, surely — is there more of it?
PAGE. My lord, it's only just begun.
SLY. It's an excellent piece of work, madam lady — I wish it were over!
[_They sit and watch._]

chapters.title: Act 1, Scene 2 — Padua. Before Hortensio’s house
paragraphs: Enter Petruchio and his servant Grumio.

PETRUCHIO. Verona, I take my leave of you for a while, to visit my friends in Padua — but above all, my best loved and most trusted friend, Hortensio. I believe this is his house. Here, Grumio, knock, I say.
GRUMIO. Knock, sir? Knock whom? Has somebody insulted your worship?
PETRUCHIO. Villain, I said — knock here for me, and do it soundly.
GRUMIO. Knock you here, sir? Why, sir — what am I, sir, that I should knock you here, sir?
PETRUCHIO. Villain, I say — knock me at this gate; and rap me well, or I'll knock your knave's skull.
GRUMIO. My master is in a quarrelsome mood. If I knock you first, then I'll know who's worse off after.
PETRUCHIO. Won't you do it? Honestly, fellow, if you won't knock, I'll ring it — I'll try how you can sol, fa, and sing it.
[_He wrings Grumio by the ears._]
GRUMIO. Help, masters, help! My master is mad.
PETRUCHIO. Now knock when I tell you to, you wretched villain!
Enter Hortensio.
HORTENSIO. Hey now! What's going on? My old friend Grumio! And my good friend Petruchio! How are you all in Verona?
PETRUCHIO. Signior Hortensio, have you come to break up the fight? _Con tutto il cuore ben trovato_, I may say.
HORTENSIO. _Alla nostra casa ben venuto; molto honorato signor mio Petruchio._ Get up, Grumio, get up — we'll settle this quarrel.

GRUMIO. No, sir, it doesn't matter what he claims in Latin. If this isn't a lawful cause for me to leave his service, look here, sir — he ordered me to knock him and rap him soundly, sir. Well, was that fitting for a servant to do to his master? Who, maybe, for all I see, is two-and-thirty and a little off. I wish to God I'd knocked him soundly first — then Grumio wouldn't be the worse off.
PETRUCHIO. A senseless villain! Good Hortensio, I told the rascal to knock on your gate, and I couldn't, for the life of me, get him to do it.
GRUMIO. Knock on the gate! Oh heavens! Didn't you say these very words: 'Fellow, knock me here, rap me here, knock me well, and knock me soundly'? And now you come with 'knocking on the gate'?
PETRUCHIO. Fellow, be gone, or stop talking — I advise you.

HORTENSIO. Petruchio, calm down — I'll vouch for Grumio. Look, this is a heavy quarrel between him and you — your old, trusty, pleasant servant Grumio. And tell me now, sweet friend — what happy wind blows you to Padua from old Verona?

PETRUCHIO. The same wind that scatters young men across the world to seek their fortunes farther from home, where there's little experience to be had. In short, Signior Hortensio, here's where I stand: Antonio, my father, has died, and I've thrust myself into this maze, hoping to marry and prosper as well as I can. I have coins in my purse and property at home, and I've come abroad to see the world.

HORTENSIO. Petruchio, shall I get straight to the point with you, then, and wish you onto a shrewish, ill-favoured wife? You wouldn't thank me much for the advice. And yet I'll guarantee she'll be rich — very rich. But you're too much my friend — I won't wish her on you.

PETRUCHIO. Signior Hortensio, between friends like us, few words are needed. So if you know one rich enough to be Petruchio's wife — since wealth is the burden of my wooing dance — let her be as foul as Florentius's love, as old as Sibyl, and as vicious and shrewish as Socrates's Xanthippe or worse, she won't move me, or at least won't blunt the edge of my desire, were she as rough as the swelling Adriatic seas. I've come to marry wealthily in Padua; if wealthily, then happily in Padua.

GRUMIO. There you go, sir — he's telling you flat out what's on his mind. Give him enough gold and marry him off to a puppet or an aglet-doll, or an old hag without a tooth in her head, though she has as many diseases as fifty-two horses — nothing's wrong, as long as the money comes with it.

HORTENSIO. Petruchio, since we've gone this far, I'll continue what I started as a joke. I can, Petruchio, help you to a wife with wealth enough, and she's young and beautiful, raised as well as a gentlewoman should be. Her only fault — and that's faults enough — is that she's intolerably shrewish, and so unreasonably wilful and stubborn that, were my fortune far worse than it is, I wouldn't marry her for a mine of gold.
PETRUCHIO. Hortensio, hush! You don't know what gold can do. Just tell me her father's name, and that's enough — I'll board her, though she rails as loud as thunder when the autumn clouds split.
HORTENSIO. Her father is Baptista Minola, a friendly and courteous gentleman. Her name is Katherina Minola, famous in Padua for her scolding tongue.

PETRUCHIO. I know her father, though I don't know her. And he knew my late father well. I won't sleep, Hortensio, until I see her. So let me be this blunt with you — I'll leave you on this first encounter, unless you'll come along with me.

GRUMIO. Please, sir, let him go while the mood is on him. On my word, if she knew him as well as I do, she'd realize scolding would do little good on him. She may call him half a dozen knaves or so — but that's nothing. Once he starts, he'll rail with his rope-tricks. I'll tell you what, sir — if she stands up to him even a little, he'll throw such a figure of speech in her face that he'll disfigure her with it, so she won't have any more eyes to see with than a cat. You don't know him, sir.

HORTENSIO. Wait, Petruchio — I must go with you, because in Baptista's keeping is my treasure. He holds the jewel of my life — his youngest daughter, beautiful Bianca — and he keeps her from me and others, suitors to her and rivals in my love. He thinks it impossible, given the defects I just rehearsed, that Katherina will ever be wooed. So Baptista has issued this order: no one shall have access to Bianca until Katherine the shrew has got a husband.
GRUMIO. Katherine the shrew! Of all titles for a girl, the worst.

HORTENSIO. Now my friend Petruchio shall do me a favour, and present me disguised in sober robes to old Baptista as a music master, well versed in music, to instruct Bianca — so that by this scheme I may at least have leave and leisure to make love to her, and court her unsuspected, by herself.
GRUMIO. No knavery here! See how, to fool the old folks, the young folks lay their heads together!
Enter Gremio and Lucentio disguised, with books under his arm.
Master, master, look about you — who goes there, ha?
HORTENSIO. Quiet, Grumio! It's the rival for my love. Petruchio, stand aside a moment.
GRUMIO. A handsome young lad, and an amorous one!

GREMIO. Oh! Very well — I've looked over the list. Listen, sir — I'll have them very handsomely bound. All books of love, mind you — see to it. And don't read any other kinds of lecture to her. You understand me. Beyond and besides Signior Baptista's generosity, I'll add to it with a tip. Take your papers too, and have them very well perfumed — for she they're going to is sweeter than perfume itself. What will you read to her?

LUCENTIO. Whatever I read to her, I'll plead for you, as for my patron, you can rest assured — as firmly as if you yourself were still in my place. Yes, and perhaps with more successful words than you, unless you were a scholar, sir.
GREMIO. Oh! This learning — what a thing it is!
GRUMIO. Oh! This woodcock — what an ass he is!
PETRUCHIO. Quiet, fellow!
HORTENSIO. Grumio, hush! God save you, Signior Gremio!

GREMIO. And you are well met, Signior Hortensio. Can you guess where I'm going? To Baptista Minola. I promised to enquire carefully about a schoolmaster for fair Bianca, and by good fortune I've landed well on this young man — for learning and behaviour fit for her purpose, well read in poetry and other books, good ones, I guarantee.
HORTENSIO. That's good. And I've met a gentleman who has promised to help me to another — a fine musician to instruct our lady. So I won't be a bit behind in duty to fair Bianca, so beloved of me.
GREMIO. Beloved of me — and that my deeds shall prove.
GRUMIO.
[_Aside._] And that his moneybags shall prove.

HORTENSIO. Gremio, this isn't the time to air our love. Listen — if you speak fairly to me, I'll tell you news that's equally good for both of us. Here is a gentleman I met by chance, who, on an agreement to his liking from us, will undertake to woo cursed Katherine — yes, and to marry her, if her dowry pleases him.
GREMIO. Well said — well done is even better. Hortensio, have you told him all her faults?
PETRUCHIO. I know she's an irritating brawling scold. If that's all, gentlemen, I see no harm.
GREMIO. No? You say that, friend? Where are you from?
PETRUCHIO. Born in Verona, son of old Antonio. My father is dead, my fortune lives for me — and I hope to see good days and many of them.

GREMIO. Oh sir, such a life with such a wife would be remarkable! But if you have the stomach for it, then go to it, in God's name — you'll have me assisting you in everything. But will you really woo this wildcat?
PETRUCHIO. Will I live?
GRUMIO. Will he woo her? Yes — or I'll hang her.

PETRUCHIO. Why did I come here, if not for that purpose? Do you think a little din can daunt my ears? Haven't I in my time heard lions roar? Haven't I heard the sea, puffed up with winds, rage like an angry boar slick with sweat? Haven't I heard great cannons in the field, and heaven's artillery thunder in the skies? Haven't I in pitched battle heard loud alarms, neighing horses, and trumpets' clang? And you tell me about a woman's tongue, which doesn't strike the ear half as hard as a chestnut popping in a farmer's fire? Pah, pah! Scare boys with bogeymen.
GRUMIO.
[_Aside_] Because he fears none.
GREMIO. Hortensio, listen — this gentleman has happily arrived, I think, for his own good and yours.
HORTENSIO. I promised we'd be contributors and cover his costs of wooing, whatever they are.
GREMIO. And so we will, provided he wins her.
GRUMIO. I wish I were as sure of a good dinner.
Enter Tranio splendidly dressed, with Biondello.
TRANIO. Gentlemen, God save you! If I may be so bold — tell me, I beg, which is the quickest way to the house of Signior Baptista Minola?
BIONDELLO. The man with the two fair daughters — is that the one you mean?
TRANIO. The very one, Biondello!
GREMIO. Look here, sir — you don't mean her, do you—
TRANIO. Perhaps him and her, sir — what's it to you?
PETRUCHIO. Not her that scolds, sir — at any cost, I beg.
TRANIO. I love no scolds, sir. Biondello, let's go.
LUCENTIO.
[_Aside_] Well begun, Tranio.
HORTENSIO. Sir, a word before you go. Are you a suitor to the girl you speak of, yes or no?
TRANIO. And if I am, sir — is that any offence?
GREMIO. No — if without more words you'll get yourself out of here.
TRANIO. Why, sir, please — aren't the streets as free for me as for you?
GREMIO. But she is not.
TRANIO. For what reason, I beg you?
GREMIO. For this reason, if you must know — she's the chosen love of Signior Gremio.
HORTENSIO. And she's the chosen of Signior Hortensio.

TRANIO. Easy, gentlemen! If you're gentlemen, give me this courtesy — hear me out patiently. Baptista is a noble gentleman, and my father is not entirely unknown to him. And were his daughter even fairer than she is, she might have more suitors — and me for one. Fair Leda's daughter had a thousand wooers — surely one more may have fair Bianca. And so she shall: Lucentio will be one, though Paris himself came hoping to win alone.
GREMIO. What — this gentleman will out-talk us all.
LUCENTIO. Sir, give him his head — I know he'll prove a worn-out nag.
PETRUCHIO. Hortensio, what's the point of all these words?
HORTENSIO. Sir, let me be so bold as to ask — have you ever seen Baptista's daughter?
TRANIO. No, sir, but I hear that he has two — the one as famous for a scolding tongue as the other is for beautiful modesty.
PETRUCHIO. Sir, sir — the first is for me. Let her pass.
GREMIO. Yes — leave that labour to great Hercules, and let it count as more than Alcides' twelve.

PETRUCHIO. Sir, understand this from me, truly: the youngest daughter, the one you're after — her father keeps her from all access to suitors, and won't promise her to any man until the elder sister is first married. The younger is free then, and not before.

TRANIO. If that's so, sir, and you are the man who must serve us all — and me among the rest — then if you break the ice and pull this off, achieve the elder and set the younger free for our access, whoever's lucky enough to have her won't be so graceless as to be ungrateful.
HORTENSIO. Sir, you speak well, and you understand it well. And since you declare yourself a suitor, you must, as we do, show gratitude to this gentleman — to whom we'll all be generally indebted.

TRANIO. Sir, I'll not be slack. As proof of it — if it pleases you, let's arrange this afternoon, and drink toasts to our lady's health, and do as adversaries do in law: fight mightily, but eat and drink as friends.
GRUMIO, BIONDELLO. Oh, excellent suggestion! Fellows, let's be off.
HORTENSIO. The suggestion is good indeed — so be it. Petruchio, I shall be your _ben venuto_.
[_Exeunt._]

chapters.title: Act 2, Scene 1 — Padua. A room in Baptista’s house
paragraphs: Enter Katherina and Bianca.

BIANCA. Good sister, don't wrong me — and don't wrong yourself — by making a bondmaid and a slave of me. I won't stand for that. But as for these other trinkets, untie my hands and I'll pull them off myself — yes, all my clothes, down to my petticoat. Or whatever you order me to do, I will, since I know my duty to my elders.
KATHERINA. Of all your suitors here, I order you to tell me which one you love best. See that you don't pretend.
BIANCA. Believe me, sister, of all the men alive, I have never yet seen that special face that I could care for more than any other.
KATHERINA. Hussy, you're lying. Isn't it Hortensio?
BIANCA. If you fancy him, sister, then I swear right here, I'll plead your case for you so that you can have him.
KATHERINA. Oh! Then maybe you fancy riches more — you'd take Gremio to keep you in fine things.
BIANCA. Is it on his account that you envy me so? No, then you're joking. And now I clearly see you've been joking with me all this time. Please, sister Kate, untie my hands.
KATHERINA. If that was a joke, then all the rest was too.
[_Strikes her._]
Enter Baptista.

BAPTISTA. Why, what's all this, madam! Where does this insolence come from? Bianca, stand aside. Poor girl — she's weeping. Go work on your needlework. Don't meddle with her. For shame, you wretch with a devilish spirit — why do you wrong her, who never wronged you? When did she ever cross you with a bitter word?
KATHERINA. Her silence mocks me, and I'll be avenged.
[_Flies after Bianca._]
BAPTISTA. What — in my sight? Bianca, get inside.
[_Exit Bianca._]

KATHERINA. What — you won't allow me anything? No, now I see: she's your treasure, she must have a husband. I shall dance barefoot on her wedding day, and, for your love of her, lead apes in hell. Don't talk to me. I'll go sit and weep until I can find an occasion for revenge.
[_Exit._]
BAPTISTA. Was ever a gentleman so grieved as I? But who comes here?
Enter Gremio, with Lucentio in the dress of a humble man; Petruchio, with Hortensio as a musician; and Tranio, with Biondello carrying a lute and books.
GREMIO. Good morning, neighbour Baptista.
BAPTISTA. Good morning, neighbour Gremio. God save you, gentlemen!
PETRUCHIO. And you, good sir! Tell me — don't you have a daughter called Katherina, fair and virtuous?
BAPTISTA. I have a daughter, sir, called Katherina.
GREMIO. You're too blunt — go about it properly.

PETRUCHIO. You wrong me, Signior Gremio — let me speak. I'm a gentleman of Verona, sir, who, having heard of her beauty and her wit, her friendliness and bashful modesty, her remarkable qualities and mild behaviour, am bold enough to present myself as a forward guest in your house — to let my eye witness the report I've so often heard. And as an entrance fee for my reception, I present you with a man of mine,
[_Presenting Hortensio._]
skilled in music and mathematics, to instruct her fully in those sciences, in which I know she is not ignorant. Accept him, or else you wrong me. His name is Licio, born in Mantua.
BAPTISTA. You're welcome, sir, and he for your good sake. But as for my daughter Katherine — this much I know: she's not for your purpose, the more's my grief.
PETRUCHIO. I see you don't mean to part with her. Or else you don't enjoy my company.
BAPTISTA. Don't mistake me — I speak only as I find. Where are you from, sir? What may I call you?
PETRUCHIO. Petruchio is my name, Antonio's son — a man well known throughout all Italy.
BAPTISTA. I know him well — you're welcome for his sake.
GREMIO. With respect to your tale, Petruchio, please — let those of us who are poor petitioners speak too. _Backare!_ You're remarkably pushy.
PETRUCHIO. Oh, forgive me, Signior Gremio — I'd like to be doing.

GREMIO. No doubt about it, sir — but you'll curse your wooing. Neighbour, this gift is very welcome, I'm sure. To show similar kindness, I myself, who have been more kindly obliged to you than anyone, freely give you this young scholar,
[_Presenting Lucentio._]
who has long been studying at Rheims — as skilled in Greek, Latin, and other languages as the other in music and mathematics. His name is Cambio — please accept his service.
BAPTISTA. A thousand thanks, Signior Gremio — welcome, good Cambio. [_To Tranio._] But, kind sir, I think you walk like a stranger. May I be so bold as to ask the reason for your visit?

TRANIO. Forgive me, sir — the boldness is my own. Being a stranger in this city, I am making myself a suitor to your daughter — to Bianca, fair and virtuous. Nor is your firm resolution unknown to me, concerning the preference for the eldest sister. This liberty is all I ask: that, given my parentage, I may be welcome among the others who woo, with the same free access and favour as the rest. And, toward the education of your daughters, I here present a simple instrument and this small bundle of Greek and Latin books. If you accept them, then their worth is great.
BAPTISTA. Lucentio is your name — from where, please?
TRANIO. From Pisa, sir — son to Vincentio.
BAPTISTA. A man of consequence in Pisa — by reputation I know him well. You are very welcome, sir.
[_To Hortensio._] You take the lute,
[_To Lucentio._] and you take the set of books.
You'll go see your pupils right away. Hey, inside!
Enter a Servant.
Fellow, lead these gentlemen to my daughters, and tell them both that these are their tutors. Tell them to treat them well.
[_Exeunt Servant with Hortensio, Lucentio and Biondello._]
We'll go take a little walk in the orchard, and then to dinner. You are exceedingly welcome — so consider yourselves so, all of you, please.

PETRUCHIO. Signior Baptista, my business demands haste, and I can't come to woo every day. You knew my father well, and through him me — sole heir to all his lands and goods, which I've improved rather than reduced. So tell me: if I win your daughter's love, what dowry shall I have with her in marriage?
BAPTISTA. After my death, half my lands — and in immediate possession, twenty thousand crowns.

PETRUCHIO. And for that dowry, I will assure her — her widow's portion, should she survive me — in all my lands and leases whatsoever. So let detailed contracts be drawn between us, so that the agreements may be kept on both sides.
BAPTISTA. Yes — once the special thing is well secured. That is, her love. For that's the whole of it.

PETRUCHIO. Why, that's nothing — for I tell you, father, I am as firm as she is proud-minded. And where two raging fires meet, they consume the very thing that feeds their fury. Though a little fire grows large with a little wind, extreme gusts will blow fire and all clear out. So I am to her, and so she yields to me — for I am rough, and don't woo like a baby.
BAPTISTA. May your wooing go well, and your speed be happy! But arm yourself for some unhappy words.
PETRUCHIO. Yes — proof against them, like mountains against winds: they don't shake, though winds blow forever.
Re-enter Hortensio, with his head bashed.
BAPTISTA. What now, my friend! Why do you look so pale?
HORTENSIO. From fear, I promise you — if I look pale.
BAPTISTA. What — will my daughter make a good musician?
HORTENSIO. I think she'll sooner make a soldier. Iron may hold up with her — but never lutes.
BAPTISTA. Why — so you can't break her in on the lute?

HORTENSIO. Why, no — for she has broken the lute on me. I just told her she'd mistaken her frets and bent her hand to teach her fingering, when, with a most impatient and devilish spirit, 'Frets, do you call these?' she said — 'I'll fret with them!' And with that word she struck me on the head, and my skull went through the instrument. There I stood amazed for a while, as in a pillory, looking through the lute — while she called me rascal fiddler and twanging Jack, with twenty other vile names, as if she'd studied how to abuse me.
PETRUCHIO. By all the world, she's a lively wench! I love her ten times more than I ever did. Oh, how I long to have a chat with her!
BAPTISTA.
[_To Hortensio._] Well, come along with me, and don't be so put out.
Carry on practising with my younger daughter. She's quick to learn, and grateful for kindness. Signior Petruchio, will you come with us, or shall I send my daughter Kate to you?
PETRUCHIO. Please do.
[_Exeunt Baptista, Gremio, Tranio and Hortensio._]

I'll wait for her here, and woo her with some spirit when she comes. Say that she rails — why, then I'll tell her plainly she sings as sweetly as a nightingale. Say she frowns — I'll say she looks as bright as morning roses freshly washed with dew. Say she stays silent and won't speak a word — then I'll praise her fluency and say she utters piercing eloquence. If she tells me to clear off, I'll thank her as though she begged me stay with her a week. If she refuses to marry, I'll demand the date when I'll cry the banns, and when we'll be married. But here she comes — now, Petruchio, speak.
Enter Katherina.
Good morning, Kate — that's your name, I hear.
KATHERINA. You've heard correctly — but a little hard of hearing. They call me Katherine, those who speak of me.

PETRUCHIO. You lie, in fact, for you're called plain Kate, and bonny Kate, and sometimes Kate the shrew. But, Kate, the prettiest Kate in Christendom — Kate of Kate Hall, my super-dainty Kate — for all dainties are Kates — and therefore, Kate, take this from me, Kate of my consolation: hearing your mildness praised in every town, your virtues spoken of, and your beauty rumoured — yet not as deeply as you deserve — I am moved to woo you for my wife.
KATHERINA. Moved! In good time. Let whoever moved you here remove you again. I knew you the first moment — you're a moveable.
PETRUCHIO. Why — what's a moveable?
KATHERINA. A joint-stool.
PETRUCHIO. You've hit it. Come, sit on me.
KATHERINA. Asses are made to bear — and so are you.
PETRUCHIO. Women are made to bear — and so are you.
KATHERINA. No such jade as to bear you, if you mean me.
PETRUCHIO. Alas, good Kate — I won't burden you. For, knowing you to be only young and light—
KATHERINA. Too light for such a swain as you to catch. And yet as heavy as my weight should be.
PETRUCHIO. Should be! Should buzz!
KATHERINA. Well caught — and like a buzzard.
PETRUCHIO. Oh, slow-winged turtle-dove — shall a buzzard take you?
KATHERINA. Yes — for a turtle, just as he takes a buzzard.
PETRUCHIO. Come now, wasp — honestly, you're too angry.
KATHERINA. If I'm waspish, you'd best beware my sting.
PETRUCHIO. My remedy then is to pluck it out.
KATHERINA. Yes — if the fool could find where it lies.
PETRUCHIO. Who doesn't know where a wasp wears its sting? In its tail.
KATHERINA. In its tongue.
PETRUCHIO. Whose tongue?
KATHERINA. Yours, if you go telling tales. And so farewell.
PETRUCHIO. What — with my tongue in your tail? No, come back, good Kate. I'm a gentleman.
KATHERINA. I'll test that.
[_Striking him._]
PETRUCHIO. I swear I'll cuff you if you strike again.
KATHERINA. So you may lose your arms — your coat of arms. If you strike me, you're no gentleman. And if no gentleman, then no arms.
PETRUCHIO. A herald, Kate? Oh — enter me in your books.
KATHERINA. What's your crest — a coxcomb?
PETRUCHIO. A combless cock, so long as Kate will be my hen.
KATHERINA. No cock of mine — you crow too like a coward.
PETRUCHIO. No, come, Kate, come — you mustn't look so sour.
KATHERINA. That's my fashion when I see a crab.
PETRUCHIO. Why, there's no crab here — so don't look sour.
KATHERINA. There is, there is.
PETRUCHIO. Then show it to me.
KATHERINA. If I had a mirror, I would.
PETRUCHIO. What — you mean my face?
KATHERINA. Sharp aim for such a young one.
PETRUCHIO. Now, by Saint George, I'm too young for you.
KATHERINA. Yet you're withered.
PETRUCHIO. With cares.
KATHERINA. I don't care.
PETRUCHIO. No, listen, Kate — truly, you won't escape so.
KATHERINA. I rile you if I stay. Let me go.

PETRUCHIO. No, not in the slightest — I find you exceedingly gentle. I was told you were rough, and coy, and sullen — and now I find that report is a complete liar. For you're pleasant, playful, exceedingly courteous, but slow in speech — yet sweet as springtime flowers. You can't frown, you can't look askance, nor bite your lip as angry wenches do, nor do you take pleasure in being contrary in talk. No — you entertain your wooers with mildness, with gentle conversation, soft and friendly. Why does the world report that Kate limps? Oh, slanderous world! Kate is straight and slender like the hazel-twig, and as brown in colour as hazel-nuts, and sweeter than the kernels. Oh — let me see you walk: you don't limp at all.
KATHERINA. Go on, fool — and command whoever you keep.
PETRUCHIO. Did ever Diana so grace a grove as Kate this room with her princely gait? Oh, you be Diana, and let her be Kate — and then let Kate be chaste, and Diana sportive!
KATHERINA. Where did you study all this elegant speech?
PETRUCHIO. It's improvised — from my mother-wit.
KATHERINA. A witty mother! Witless otherwise her son.
PETRUCHIO. Am I not wise?
KATHERINA. Yes — keep yourself warm.

PETRUCHIO. Indeed, that's what I intend, sweet Katherine — in your bed. So setting all this chat aside, plainly: your father has consented that you shall be my wife. Your dowry is agreed. And whether you will or not, I will marry you. Now, Kate, I'm a husband for your purpose — for, by this light, by which I see your beauty — your beauty that makes me like you so well — you must be married to no man but me. For I am the one born to tame you, Kate, and bring you from a wild Kate to a Kate as conformable as other household Kates.
Re-enter Baptista, Gremio and Tranio.
Here comes your father. Don't deny it — I must and will have Katherine as my wife.
BAPTISTA. Now, Signior Petruchio, how do you fare with my daughter?
PETRUCHIO. How but well, sir? How but well? It would be impossible for me to fare badly.
BAPTISTA. Why, what's this, daughter Katherine — in the dumps?

KATHERINA. You call me daughter? Now I assure you, you have shown a tender fatherly regard, wishing me wed to one half lunatic — a mad-cap ruffian and a swearing Jack, who thinks he can bluff his way through with oaths.

PETRUCHIO. Father, the situation is this: you, and all the world that has talked about her, have talked of her wrongly. If she is shrewish, it's a deliberate strategy — for she's not stubborn, but as modest as a dove. She's not hot-tempered, but as temperate as the morning. For patience she'll prove a second Griselda, and Roman Lucrece for her chastity. And to conclude, we have agreed so well together that Sunday is the wedding day.
KATHERINA. I'll see you hanged on Sunday first.
GREMIO. Listen, Petruchio — she says she'll see you hanged first.
TRANIO. Is this your success? Well — goodnight to our part of it!

PETRUCHIO. Be patient, gentlemen. I'm choosing her for myself. If she and I are pleased, what's that to you? It's been bargained between the two of us, in private, that she'll still play the shrew in company. I tell you, it's incredible to believe how much she loves me. Oh, the sweetest Kate — she hung about my neck, and kiss on kiss she came at me so fast, swearing oath on oath, that in a moment she won me to her love. Oh, you are novices. It's a sight to see, when men and women are alone, how tame a milksop wretch can make the worst shrew. Give me your hand, Kate — I'm off to Venice, to buy clothes for the wedding day. Prepare the feast, father, and invite the guests. I'll make sure my Katherine is finely dressed.
BAPTISTA. I don't know what to say — but give me your hands. God send you joy, Petruchio! It's a match.
GREMIO, TRANIO. Amen, say we — we'll be witnesses.
PETRUCHIO. Father, and wife, and gentlemen, farewell. I'm off to Venice — Sunday is coming fast. We'll have rings and things, and fine clothes. And kiss me, Kate — we'll be married on Sunday.
[_Exeunt Petruchio and Katherina, separately._]
GREMIO. Was ever a match closed so suddenly?
BAPTISTA. Honestly, gentlemen, now I'm playing a merchant's part, and venturing recklessly on a desperate market.
TRANIO. The merchandise was sitting and spoiling on your hands. It'll bring you gain, or be lost at sea.
BAPTISTA. The gain I'm after is peace in the match.
GREMIO. No doubt he's got himself a quiet catch. But now, Baptista, to your younger daughter — this is the day we've long looked forward to. I am your neighbour, and was suitor first.
TRANIO. And I am one who loves Bianca more than words can tell or your thoughts can guess.
GREMIO. Youngster, you can't love as dearly as I.
TRANIO. Greybeard, your love is freezing.
GREMIO. But yours fries. Skipper, stand back — it's age that nourishes.
TRANIO. But it's youth that flourishes in ladies' eyes.

BAPTISTA. Settle down, gentlemen — I'll resolve this dispute. It's deeds that must win the prize: whichever of you can guarantee my daughter the largest settlement shall have my Bianca's love. Say, Signior Gremio, what can you guarantee her?

GREMIO. First, as you know, my house in town is richly furnished with plate and gold — basins and ewers to wash her dainty hands. My hangings are all Tyrian tapestry; in ivory coffers I've stuffed my crowns. In cypress chests, my counterpane tapestries, costly clothes, tents, and canopies, fine linen, Turkish cushions embossed with pearl, valances of Venetian gold needlework, pewter and brass, and everything that belongs to a house or housekeeping. Then, at my farm, I have a hundred milk-cows at the pail, six score fat oxen standing in my stalls, and everything else proportionate to this. I'm getting on in years, I must admit. And if I die tomorrow, all this is hers — provided that while I live, she'll be mine alone.

TRANIO. That 'alone' was well placed. Sir, listen to me: I am my father's heir and only son. If I may have your daughter as my wife, I'll leave her three or four houses, every one as good within rich Pisa's walls as any old Signior Gremio has in Padua — plus two thousand ducats a year from fruitful land, all of which shall be her settlement. What — have I pinched you, Signior Gremio?
GREMIO. Two thousand ducats a year from land! My total land doesn't come to that much. She shall have that, plus an argosy now lying in the Marseilles roads. What — have I choked you with an argosy?
TRANIO. Gremio, it's known my father has no less than three great argosies, plus two galliasses, and twelve tight galleys. I'll guarantee her these — and twice as much as whatever you offer next.
GREMIO. No, I've offered all I have — no more. And she can have no more than all I have. If you like me, she shall have me and mine.
TRANIO. Why, then the girl is mine against all the world, by your firm promise. Gremio is outbid.

BAPTISTA. I must admit your offer is the best. And let your father guarantee her this — and she's your own. Otherwise, you'll have to forgive me. If you were to die before him, where would her settlement be?
TRANIO. That's just a quibble — he's old, I'm young.
GREMIO. And can't young men die as well as old?

BAPTISTA. Well, gentlemen, this is what I've decided. Next Sunday, as you know, my daughter Katherine is to be married. Now, on the following Sunday, Bianca shall be your bride, if you provide this guarantee. If not, to Signior Gremio. And so I take my leave, and thank you both.
GREMIO. Farewell, good neighbour.
[_Exit Baptista._]

Now, I don't fear you. Look here, young gamester — your father would be a fool to give you everything, and in his old age sit at the foot of your table. Pah, nonsense! An old Italian fox is not so kind, my boy.
[_Exit._]

TRANIO. A curse on your crafty withered hide! Yet I've faced him down with a card worth ten. It's in my head to do my master good. I see no reason why supposed Lucentio shouldn't get himself a father — called supposed Vincentio. And that's a wonder: fathers ordinarily beget their children — but in this case of wooing, a child shall beget a sire, if my cunning doesn't fail me.
[_Exit._]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 1 — Padua. A room in Baptista’s house
paragraphs: Enter Lucentio, Hortensio and Bianca.
LUCENTIO. Fiddler, hold off — you're getting too forward, sir. Have you so soon forgotten the welcome her sister Katherine treated you to?
HORTENSIO. But, quibbling pedant, this lady is the patroness of heavenly harmony. So let me have priority — and when we've spent an hour on music, your lecture shall have the same time.

LUCENTIO. Ridiculous ass — you never read far enough to know why music was invented! Wasn't it to refresh a man's mind after his studies or his usual labour? So let me read philosophy, and while I pause, serve up your harmony.
HORTENSIO. Fellow, I won't put up with these provocations of yours.

BIANCA. Why, gentlemen, you wrong me twice over, by quarrelling over what lies in my choice. I'm not a schoolboy under threat of the rod — I won't be tied to set hours or appointed times. I'll learn my lessons as I please. And, to cut off all strife, here let us sit down. You take your instrument, play in the meantime — his lecture will be finished before you have tuned.
HORTENSIO. You'll leave his lecture when I'm in tune?
[_Retires._]
LUCENTIO. That'll be never. Tune your instrument.
BIANCA. Where did we leave off?
LUCENTIO. Here, madam: _Hic ibat Simois; hic est Sigeia tellus; Hic steterat Priami regia celsa senis._
BIANCA. Translate it.

LUCENTIO. _Hic ibat_, as I told you before; _Simois_, I am Lucentio; _hic est_, son to Vincentio of Pisa; _Sigeia tellus_, disguised this way to win your love; _Hic steterat_, and that Lucentio who comes wooing; _Priami_, is my man Tranio; _regia_, taking my place; _celsa senis_, so that we might fool the old pantaloon.
HORTENSIO. [_Returning._] Madam, my instrument is in tune.
BIANCA. Let's hear.
[_Hortensio plays._]
Oh, ugh! The treble jars.
LUCENTIO. Spit in the hole, man, and tune it again.

BIANCA. Now let me see if I can translate it: _Hic ibat Simois_, I don't know you; _hic est Sigeia tellus_, I don't trust you; _Hic steterat Priami_, take care he doesn't hear us; _regia_, don't presume; _celsa senis_, don't despair.
HORTENSIO. Madam, it's in tune now.
LUCENTIO. All but the bass.
HORTENSIO. The bass is right — it's the base knave that jars.
[_Aside_] How fiery and forward our pedant is!
Now, on my life, the rascal is courting my love. Little pedant, I'll watch you better from now on.
BIANCA. In time I may believe — but I still mistrust.
LUCENTIO. Don't mistrust it — for sure, Æacides was Ajax, named so from his grandfather.

BIANCA. I must believe my master — otherwise, I promise you, I'd still be arguing about that doubt. But let it rest. Now, Licio, to you. Good master, please don't take it amiss that I've been so playful with both of you.
HORTENSIO.
[_To Lucentio_] You may go take a walk and give me some space.
My lessons don't make music in three parts.
LUCENTIO. Are you so strict, sir? Well, I must wait.
[_Aside_] And keep an eye out too. Unless I'm mistaken,
our fine musician is growing amorous.

HORTENSIO. Madam, before you touch the instrument, to learn the order of my fingering, I must begin with the basics of the art. I'll teach you the gamut in a quicker fashion — more pleasant, pithy, and effective than has been taught by anyone in my trade. And there it is in writing, neatly drawn out.
BIANCA. Why, I'm past the gamut long ago.
HORTENSIO. Yet read the gamut of Hortensio.

BIANCA. _Gamut_ I am, the foundation of all harmony; _A re_, to plead Hortensio's passion; _B mi_, Bianca, take him for your lord; _C fa ut_, who loves with all his heart; _D sol re_, one key, two notes I have; _E la mi_, show pity or I die. You call this a gamut? Pah, I don't like it. Old fashions please me best — I'm not so fastidious as to swap true rules for odd inventions.
Enter a Servant.
SERVANT. Mistress, your father asks you to leave your books and help to dress up your sister's chamber. You know tomorrow is the wedding day.
BIANCA. Farewell, sweet masters, both of you. I must be off.
[_Exeunt Bianca and Servant._]
LUCENTIO. Truly, mistress, then I have no reason to stay.
[_Exit._]

HORTENSIO. But I do have reason to pry into this pedant. He looks to me as though he were in love. Yet if your thoughts, Bianca, are so cheap as to cast your wandering eyes on every commoner — let anyone who wants you seize you. If I once catch you straying, Hortensio will be quits with you by switching too.
[_Exit._]

chapters.title: Act 3, Scene 2 — The same. Before Baptista’s house
paragraphs: Enter Baptista, Gremio, Tranio, Katherina, Bianca, Lucentio and Attendants.

BAPTISTA. [_To Tranio._] Signior Lucentio, this is the appointed day when Katherine and Petruchio are to be married, and yet we hear nothing of our son-in-law. What will people say? What a mockery this will be — to lack a bridegroom while the priest waits to perform the marriage ceremony! What does Lucentio say to this shame of ours?

KATHERINA. No shame but mine. I must, indeed, be forced to give my hand, against my heart's wishes, to a mad-brained ruffian, full of malice — who wooed in a hurry and intends to marry at his leisure. I told you, didn't I — that he was a frantic fool, hiding his bitter jokes in blunt manners. And to be known as a witty man, he'll woo a thousand women, set the wedding day, make friends, invite guests, and proclaim the banns — yet never intends to marry where he has wooed. Now the world will point at poor Katherine and say, 'Look! There is mad Petruchio's wife, if he ever bothers to come and marry her.'

TRANIO. Patience, good Katherine — and Baptista too. On my life, Petruchio means only well, whatever misfortune holds him from his word. Though he's blunt, I know him to be very wise. Though he's merry, he is still honest.
KATHERINA. I wish Katherine had never seen him at all!
[_Exit weeping, followed by Bianca and others._]
BAPTISTA. Go, girl — I can't blame you for weeping now. Such an injury would vex a saint, let alone a shrew of your impatient temper.
Enter Biondello.
Master, master! News! Old news, and news of a kind you've never heard before!
BAPTISTA. Is it new and old at once? How can that be?
BIONDELLO. Why — isn't it news to hear that Petruchio is coming?
BAPTISTA. Has he come?
BIONDELLO. Why no, sir.
BAPTISTA. What then?
BIONDELLO. He is coming.
BAPTISTA. When will he be here?
BIONDELLO. When he stands where I am and sees you there.
TRANIO. But say — what about your old news?

BIONDELLO. Well, Petruchio is coming — in a new hat and an old jerkin; a pair of old breeches turned three times; a pair of boots that used to be candle-cases, one buckled, one laced; an old rusty sword taken from the town armoury, with a broken hilt and no scabbard, and two broken laces. His horse hipped, with an old moth-eaten saddle and stirrups that don't match. Beyond that, riddled with glanders and likely to drip from the spine — troubled with the lampass, infected with the fashions, full of windgalls, ridden with spavins, jaundiced with the yellows, beyond cure of the fives, ruined by staggers, gnawed by botflies, sway-backed and shoulder-shotten, knock-kneed in front, with a half-checked bit and a head-stall of sheep's leather, which, being tightened to keep him from stumbling, has often broken and is now patched with knots. One girth pieced together six times, and a woman's crupper of velvet with two letters of her name set in studs, here and there patched with packing-thread.
BAPTISTA. Who comes with him?

BIONDELLO. Oh, sir! His lackey — for all the world rigged out like the horse: with a linen stocking on one leg and a coarse boot-hose on the other, gartered with a red and blue strip; an old hat, and the trim of forty fancies stuck in for a feather. A monster, a perfect monster of apparel, and not like a Christian footboy or a gentleman's lackey at all.
TRANIO. Some odd whim has driven him to dress this way. Yet often he goes plainly enough dressed.
BAPTISTA. I'm glad he's come, however he comes.
BIONDELLO. Why, sir — he isn't coming.
BAPTISTA. Didn't you just say he's coming?
BIONDELLO. Who? That Petruchio came?
BAPTISTA. Yes — that Petruchio came.
BIONDELLO. No, sir — I'm saying his horse comes, with him on its back.
BAPTISTA. Why, that amounts to the same thing.
BIONDELLO. No, by Saint Jamy — I bet you a penny: a horse and a man are more than one, and yet not many.
Enter Petruchio and Grumio.
PETRUCHIO. Come on, where are these gallants? Who's at home?
BAPTISTA. You're welcome, sir.
PETRUCHIO. And yet I come not well.
BAPTISTA. And yet you do not limp.
TRANIO. Not so well-dressed as I'd wish you to be.

PETRUCHIO. Even if I were better, I'd still rush in like this. But where is Kate? Where is my lovely bride? How is my father? Gentlemen, you seem to frown. Why does this good company stare, as if they saw some wondrous monument, some comet, or unusual prodigy?

BAPTISTA. Why, sir — you know this is your wedding day. First we were sad, fearing you wouldn't come. Now we're sadder, because you come so unprepared. Fie! Take off this outfit — it's a shame to your standing, and an eyesore at our solemn festival.
TRANIO. And tell us what matter of importance has detained you so long from your wife, and sent you here looking so unlike yourself?

PETRUCHIO. It would be tedious to tell and harsh to hear. It's enough that I've come to keep my word, even though forced in some part to digress — which at more leisure I'll explain so well that you'll be satisfied. But where is Kate? I've stayed away too long. The morning is wearing on — it's time we were at church.
TRANIO. Don't see your bride in these disrespectful clothes. Go to my room, put on some of mine.
PETRUCHIO. Not I — believe me. This is how I'll visit her.
BAPTISTA. But, I trust, this is not how you'll marry her.

PETRUCHIO. In good faith, just like this. So have done with words. She's married to me, not to my clothes. If I could mend what she'll wear out in me as easily as I can change these poor accoutrements, it would be well for Kate, and better for me. But what a fool I am to chat with you, when I should be wishing my bride good morning, and sealing the bond with a loving kiss!
[_Exeunt Petruchio, Grumio and Biondello._]
TRANIO. There's some meaning in this mad attire. We'll persuade him, if we can, to put on better clothes before he goes to church.
BAPTISTA. I'll go after him and see how this turns out.
[_Exeunt Baptista, Gremio and Attendants._]

TRANIO. But, sir, regarding love, we still need to add her father's approval — and to bring that about, as I told your worship before, I need to get hold of a man — whoever he may be, it doesn't matter much, we'll suit him to our purpose — and he shall be Vincentio of Pisa, and provide guarantees here in Padua of greater sums than I've promised. So you'll quietly enjoy your hope, and marry sweet Bianca with consent.

LUCENTIO. Were it not that my fellow schoolmaster watches Bianca's every step so closely, I think it would be good to steal our marriage. Once that's done, let all the world say no — I'll keep what's mine in spite of all the world.

TRANIO. We'll look into that step by step, and watch for our advantage in this business. We'll outwit the greybeard, Gremio, the narrow-prying father, Minola, and the dainty musician, amorous Licio — all for my master's sake, Lucentio.
Re-enter Gremio.
Signior Gremio, are you coming from the church?
GREMIO. As gladly as ever I came home from school.
TRANIO. And are the bride and bridegroom coming home?
GREMIO. A bridegroom, you say? He's a groom indeed — a grumbling groom, and that the girl will find out.
TRANIO. Worse than her? Why, that's impossible.
GREMIO. Why, he's a devil, a devil, a very fiend.
TRANIO. Why, she's a devil, a devil, the devil's own mother.

GREMIO. Pah! She's a lamb, a dove, a fool, compared to him. I'll tell you, Sir Lucentio: when the priest was supposed to ask if Katherine should be his wife — 'Yes, by God's wounds,' he said, and swore so loud that the priest, all astonished, dropped the book. And as he stooped down again to pick it up, the mad-brained bridegroom struck him such a cuff that down fell priest and book, and book and priest. 'Now pick them up,' he said, 'if anyone wants to.'
TRANIO. What did the girl say when he stood up again?

GREMIO. She trembled and shook — because he stamped and swore as if the vicar meant to cheat him. But after many ceremonies were done, he called for wine. 'A health!' he said, as if he'd been abroad, carousing with his mates after a storm. He quaffed off the muscadel and threw the sops in the sexton's face — for no other reason than that his beard grew thin and hungry-looking, and seemed to be begging for sops as he was drinking. With that done, he took the bride about the neck and kissed her lips with such a clamorous smack that at the parting all the church echoed. And I, seeing this, came away out of sheer shame. After me, I know, the whole crowd is coming. There was never such a mad marriage. Listen, listen — I hear the minstrels playing.
[_Music plays._]
Enter Petruchio, Katherina, Bianca, Baptista, Hortensio, Grumio and Train.

PETRUCHIO. Gentlemen and friends, I thank you for your trouble. I know you planned to dine with me today, and have prepared a great spread of wedding cheer. But things being as they are, my haste calls me away — so this is where I mean to take my leave.
BAPTISTA. Is it possible you'll be off tonight?

PETRUCHIO. I must be off today, before night comes. Don't be surprised — if you knew my business, you'd urge me to go rather than stay. And, honest company, I thank you all — you who have watched me give myself away to this most patient, sweet, and virtuous wife. Dine with my father, drink a health to me. For I must go — and farewell to you all.
TRANIO. Let us beg you to stay till after dinner.
PETRUCHIO. It can't be done.
GREMIO. Let me beg you.
PETRUCHIO. It cannot be.
KATHERINA. Let me beg you.
PETRUCHIO. I am content.
KATHERINA. Content to stay?
PETRUCHIO. Content that you should beg me to stay — but not to actually stay, no matter how you beg.
KATHERINA. Now, if you love me, stay.
PETRUCHIO. Grumio, my horse!
GRUMIO. Yes, sir, they're ready — the oats have eaten the horses.

KATHERINA. No, then — do what you can, I will not go today. No, nor tomorrow — not until I please myself. The door is open, sir — there's your way. You can be off while your boots are still fresh. As for me, I won't leave until I please myself. It looks like you'll prove a fine surly groom, taking it on yourself like this so soon.
PETRUCHIO. Oh Kate! Settle down — please don't be angry.
KATHERINA. I will be angry — what does it matter to you? Father, be quiet — he shall wait until I'm ready.
GREMIO. Yes, indeed, sir — now it begins to work.
KATHERINA. Gentlemen, let's go forward to the wedding feast. I see a woman can be made a fool, if she doesn't have a spirit to resist.

PETRUCHIO. They shall go forward, Kate, at your command. Obey the bride, you who attend her. Go to the feast — revel and lord it over things. Carouse a full measure to her maidenhood. Be mad and merry, or go hang yourselves. But as for my bonny Kate — she must come with me. No — don't look big, or stamp, or stare, or fret. I will be master of what is my own. She is my goods, my chattel; she is my house, my household stuff, my field, my barn, my horse, my ox, my ass, my anything. And here she stands — touch her whoever dares. I'll bring my action against the proudest man who stops my way in Padua. Grumio — draw your weapon. We're beset by thieves. Rescue your mistress, if you're a man. Don't fear, sweet wench — they shall not touch you, Kate. I'll defend you against a million.
[_Exeunt Petruchio, Katherina and Grumio._]
BAPTISTA. No, let them go — a quiet pair, those two.
GREMIO. If they hadn't gone quickly, I'd have died laughing.
TRANIO. Of all mad matches, there was never the like.
LUCENTIO. Mistress, what's your opinion of your sister?
BIANCA. That, being mad herself, she's madly matched.
GREMIO. I guarantee, Petruchio is well and truly Kated.

BAPTISTA. Neighbours and friends — though we lack a bride and groom to fill the places at the table, you know there's no lack of sweetmeats at the feast. Lucentio, you shall fill the bridegroom's place. And let Bianca take her sister's seat.
TRANIO. Shall sweet Bianca practise how to play the bride?
BAPTISTA. She shall, Lucentio. Come, gentlemen, let's go.
[_Exeunt._]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 1 — A hall in Petruchio’s country house
paragraphs: Enter Grumio.

GRUMIO. Curse it, curse it on all tired nags, on all mad masters, and all foul roads! Was ever a man so beaten? Was ever a man so spattered? Was ever a man so weary? I'm sent ahead to make a fire, and they're coming after to warm themselves. Now, if I weren't a little pot that boils up fast, my very lips might freeze to my teeth, my tongue to the roof of my mouth, my heart in my belly, before I came near a fire to thaw me. But blowing on the fire will warm me — for, considering this weather, a taller man than me will catch cold. Hello, ho! Curtis!
Enter Curtis.
CURTIS. Who's that calling so chillily?
GRUMIO. A piece of ice — if you doubt it, you may slide from my shoulder to my heel with no greater run-up than my head and neck. A fire, good Curtis.
CURTIS. Are my master and his wife coming, Grumio?
GRUMIO. Oh yes! Curtis, yes — so fire, fire, and don't throw any water on it.
CURTIS. Is she such a hot shrew as she's reputed to be?
GRUMIO. She was, good Curtis, before this frost. But you know winter tames man, woman, and beast — it has tamed my old master, and my new mistress, and myself, fellow Curtis.
CURTIS. Away with you, you three-inch fool! I am no beast.

GRUMIO. Am I just three inches? Why, your horn is a foot — and so long am I at the very least. But will you make a fire, or shall I complain about you to our mistress, whose hand — she being now at hand — you shall soon feel, to your cold comfort, for being slow at your hot duty?
CURTIS. Please, good Grumio, tell me — how goes the world?
GRUMIO. A cold world, Curtis, in every department but yours — so fire! Do your duty, and have your due, for my master and mistress are nearly frozen to death.
CURTIS. There's fire ready. So, good Grumio — the news.
GRUMIO. Why — 'Jack boy! Ho, boy!' and as much news as you want.
CURTIS. Come on — you're so full of con tricks.

GRUMIO. Why, therefore, fire — for I've caught an extreme cold. Where's the cook? Is supper ready, the house tidied, rushes strewn, cobwebs swept, the servingmen in their new fustian and white stockings, every officer in his wedding clothes? Are the cups clean inside, the girls neat outside, and carpets laid, everything in order?
CURTIS. All ready. So please — the news.
GRUMIO. First, know that my horse is exhausted, and my master and mistress have fallen out.
CURTIS. How?
GRUMIO. Out of their saddles into the dirt — and there hangs a tale.
CURTIS. Let's have it, good Grumio.
GRUMIO. Lend me your ear.
CURTIS. Here.
GRUMIO.
[_Striking him._] There.
CURTIS. This is to feel a tale, not to hear a tale.

GRUMIO. That's why it's called a sensible tale — and this cuff was just to knock at your ear and beg for a listen. Now I begin: _Imprimis_, we came down a foul hill, my master riding behind my mistress—
CURTIS. Both on one horse?
GRUMIO. What's that to you?
CURTIS. Why — a horse.

GRUMIO. You tell the tale yourself. But if you hadn't interrupted me, you'd have heard how her horse fell, and she under her horse; you'd have heard in how miry a place, how she was filthy with mud; how he left her with the horse on top of her; how he beat me because her horse stumbled; how she waded through the mud to pull him off me; how he swore; how she prayed, who never prayed before; how I cried; how the horses ran away; how her bridle was broken; how I lost my crupper — with many other things worth remembering, which now shall die in oblivion, and you'll return inexperienced to your grave.
CURTIS. By this reckoning he's more of a shrew than she is.

GRUMIO. Yes — and that you and the proudest of you all shall find out when he comes home. But why am I talking about this? Call out Nathaniel, Joseph, Nicholas, Philip, Walter, Sugarsop, and the rest. Let their hair be smoothly combed, their blue coats brushed, and their garters of matching knit. Let them curtsy with their left legs, and not presume to touch a hair of my master's horse-tail until they kiss their hands. Are they all ready?
CURTIS. They are.
GRUMIO. Call them out.
CURTIS. Do you hear? Ho! You must meet my master to support my mistress.
GRUMIO. Why, she has a face of her own.
CURTIS. Who doesn't know that?
GRUMIO. You, it seems, since you call for company to support her.
CURTIS. I call them out to do her credit.
GRUMIO. Why, she doesn't come to borrow anything of them.
Enter four or five Servants.
NATHANIEL. Welcome home, Grumio!
PHILIP. How now, Grumio!
JOSEPH. What, Grumio!
NICHOLAS. Fellow Grumio!
NATHANIEL. How now, old lad!
GRUMIO. Welcome, you; how now, you; what, you; fellow, you — and that's enough for greetings. Now, my smart companions, is everything ready and neat?
NATHANIEL. Everything is ready. How near is our master?
GRUMIO. Right at hand — dismounted by this time. So don't — by God's passion, silence! I hear my master.
Enter Petruchio and Katherina.
PETRUCHIO. Where are these knaves? What — no man at the door to hold my stirrup or to take my horse? Where is Nathaniel, Gregory, Philip?
ALL SERVANTS. Here, here, sir; here, sir.
PETRUCHIO. Here, sir! Here, sir! Here, sir! Here, sir! You logger-headed and unpolished grooms! What — no attendance? No regard? No duty? Where is the foolish knave I sent on ahead?
GRUMIO. Here, sir — as foolish as I was before.
PETRUCHIO. You peasant lout! You whoreson malt-horse drudge! Didn't I tell you to meet me in the park, and to bring these rascal knaves along with you?

GRUMIO. Nathaniel's coat, sir, wasn't fully made. Gabriel's pumps were unpinked at the heel. There was no link to dye Peter's hat black. Walter's dagger hadn't come back from the sheath-maker. There were none decent except Adam, Ralph, and Gregory. The rest were ragged, old, and beggarly. Yet, as they are, here they are, come to meet you.
PETRUCHIO. Go, rascals, go and bring my supper in.
[_Exeunt some of the Servants._]
Where is the life that late I led? Where are those—? Sit down, Kate, and welcome. Food, food, food, food!
Re-enter Servants with supper.

Why, when, I say? — No, good sweet Kate, be merry. Off with my boots, you rogues, you villains — when? 'It was the friar of orders grey, as he forth walked on his way:' — Out, you rogue! You pull my foot askew.
[_Strikes him._]
Take that, and mind how you pull off the other one. Be merry, Kate. Some water here — what, ho! Where's my spaniel Troilus? Fellow, get yourself out and tell my cousin Ferdinand to come here.
[_Exit Servant._]
One, Kate, that you must kiss and get acquainted with. Where are my slippers? Shall I have some water? Come, Kate, and wash, and welcome with all my heart.
[_Servant lets the ewer fall. Petruchio strikes him._]
You whoreson villain! Will you drop it?
KATHERINA. Patience, please — it was an unwilling fault.
PETRUCHIO. A whoreson, beetle-headed, flap-eared knave! Come, Kate, sit down — I know you're hungry. Will you give thanks, sweet Kate, or shall I? What's this — mutton?
FIRST SERVANT. Yes.
PETRUCHIO. Who brought it?
PETER. I did.
PETRUCHIO. It's burnt — and so is all the meat. What dogs are these! Where is the rascal cook? How dared you, villains, bring it from the kitchen and serve it thus to me, who can't stand it?
[_Throws the meat, etc., at them._]
There — take it back, plates, cups, and all. You heedless blockheads and unmannered slaves! What — do you grumble? I'll deal with you in a moment.
KATHERINA. Please, husband, don't be so worked up. The meat was fine, if you'd just have been content.

PETRUCHIO. I tell you, Kate, it was burnt and dried out — and I'm specifically forbidden to touch it. It breeds bile, plants anger. Better that we both fast — since by our own nature we're choleric — than feed our temper with over-roasted flesh. Be patient — tomorrow it will be amended. And for tonight we'll fast together. Come — I'll bring you to your bridal chamber.
[_Exeunt Petruchio, Katherina and Curtis._]
NATHANIEL. Peter, did you ever see the like?
PETER. He outdoes her in her own humour.
Re-enter Curtis.
GRUMIO. Where is he?

CURTIS. In her chamber, preaching a sermon on continence to her. He rails, and swears, and scolds, until she, poor soul, doesn't know which way to stand, look, or speak — and sits like one just risen from a dream. Away, away — for he's coming this way.
[_Exeunt._]
Re-enter Petruchio.

PETRUCHIO. Thus I have politicly begun my reign — and it is my hope to end it successfully. My falcon now is keen and exceedingly empty — and till she stoops she must not be fully fed, for then she'll never look at her lure. Another method I have for taming my haggard, to make her come and know her keeper's call — that is, to watch her, as we watch these kites that flutter and beat their wings, refusing to be obedient. She ate no meat today, and shall eat none. Last night she didn't sleep, and tonight she shall not either. As with the meat, I'll find some undeserved fault about the making of the bed. Here I'll fling the pillow, there the bolster, this way the coverlet, another way the sheets — yes, and in the middle of this chaos I'll pretend that all is done in reverent care of her. And, in conclusion, she shall stay awake all night. If she happens to nod off, I'll rail and brawl, and with the clamour keep her awake. This is a way to kill a wife with kindness — and thus I'll curb her mad and headstrong humour. Whoever knows a better way to tame a shrew, let him speak now — it's charity to share.
[_Exit._]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 2 — Padua. Before Baptista’s house
paragraphs: Enter Tranio and Hortensio.
TRANIO. Is it possible, friend Licio, that Mistress Bianca cares for any man other than Lucentio? I tell you, sir, she gives me strong encouragement.
HORTENSIO. Sir, to satisfy you about what I've said, stand aside and observe the manner of his teaching.
[_They stand aside._]
Enter Bianca and Lucentio.
LUCENTIO. Now, mistress, are you profiting from what you read?
BIANCA. What is it, master, that you read? Tell me that first.
LUCENTIO. I read what I profess — _The Art of Love_.
BIANCA. And may you prove, sir, master of your art!
LUCENTIO. While you, sweet dear, prove mistress of my heart.
[_They retire._]
HORTENSIO. Fast workers, indeed! Now tell me, please — you, who dared swear that your Mistress Bianca loved no one in the world as well as Lucentio.
TRANIO. Oh, spiteful love! Inconstant womankind! I tell you, Licio, this is astonishing.

HORTENSIO. Don't be mistaken any longer — I am not Licio. Nor a musician, as I seem to be. I'm one who scorns to live in this disguise, for a woman who leaves a gentleman and makes a god of such a low fellow. Know, sir, that my name is Hortensio.

TRANIO. Signior Hortensio, I have often heard of your wholehearted affection for Bianca. And since my own eyes are now witness to her fickleness, I will, if you're willing, join you and forswear Bianca and her love forever.

HORTENSIO. See, how they kiss and court! Signior Lucentio, here is my hand, and here I firmly vow never to woo her again — and I forswear her, as someone unworthy of all the former attentions I've foolishly lavished on her.
TRANIO. And here I take the same unfeigned oath — never to marry her, even if she pleaded with me. Shame on her! See how shamelessly she courts him!

HORTENSIO. I wish all the world but him had quite forsworn her! As for me, so that I may surely keep my oath, I'll be married to a wealthy widow before three days pass — one who has loved me as long as I have loved this proud, disdainful haggard. And so farewell, Signior Lucentio. Kindness in women, not their beautiful looks, shall win my love. And so I take my leave, in the same resolution as I swore before.
[_Exit Hortensio. Lucentio and Bianca come forward._]
TRANIO. Mistress Bianca, may you be blessed with such grace as belongs to a lover's happy state! No — I've caught you napping, gentle love, and I've forsworn you along with Hortensio.
BIANCA. Tranio, you're joking — but have you both really forsworn me?
TRANIO. Mistress, we have.
LUCENTIO. Then we are rid of Licio.
TRANIO. Honestly, he'll have a lively widow now, who shall be wooed and wedded in a day.
BIANCA. God give him joy!
TRANIO. Yes — and he'll tame her.
BIANCA. So he says, Tranio.
TRANIO. Truly, he's gone off to taming-school.
BIANCA. Taming-school! What — is there such a place?
TRANIO. Yes, mistress — and Petruchio is the master. He teaches eleven and twenty long tricks for taming a shrew and charming her chattering tongue.
Enter Biondello, running.
BIONDELLO. Oh master, master! I've watched so long I'm dog-tired — but at last I've spied an ancient sort of angel coming down the hill who will serve our turn.
TRANIO. What is he, Biondello?
BIONDELLO. Master, a merchant or a pedant, I don't know which — but formal in dress, and in gait and countenance very much like a father.
LUCENTIO. And what of him, Tranio?

TRANIO. If he's credulous and believes my story, I'll make him glad to play Vincentio and give assurances to Baptista Minola as if he were the real Vincentio. Take in your love, and then leave me to it.
[_Exeunt Lucentio and Bianca._]
Enter a Pedant.
PEDANT. God save you, sir!
TRANIO. And you, sir! You are welcome. Are you travelling on far, or are you at the end of your journey?
PEDANT. Sir, at the end for a week or two. But then on further — as far as Rome. And so to Tripoli, if God grants me life.
TRANIO. What country are you from, please?
PEDANT. From Mantua.
TRANIO. From Mantua, sir? Indeed — God forbid! And come to Padua, regardless of your life?
PEDANT. My life, sir! How so, please? That sounds serious.

TRANIO. It's death for anyone from Mantua to come to Padua. Don't you know the cause? Your ships are detained at Venice. And the Duke — for a private quarrel between your Duke and him — has published and proclaimed it openly. It's a wonder — but, being only newly arrived, you might otherwise have heard it proclaimed.
PEDANT. Alas, sir! It's worse for me than that — for I have bills of exchange from Florence and must deliver them here.
TRANIO. Well, sir, to do you a courtesy, this is what I'll do — and this is what I'd advise you. First, tell me — have you ever been to Pisa?
PEDANT. Yes, sir — in Pisa I have often been. Pisa, famous for its grave citizens.
TRANIO. Among them, do you know one Vincentio?
PEDANT. I don't know him, but I have heard of him — a merchant of incomparable wealth.
TRANIO. He is my father, sir. And, truth to say, in countenance he somewhat resembles you.
BIONDELLO.
[_Aside._] As much as an apple resembles an oyster — same thing entirely.

TRANIO. To save your life in this extremity, this is the favour I'll do you for his sake. And don't count it the worst of all your fortunes that you happen to look like Sir Vincentio. You shall take on his name and credit, and in my house you shall be lodged as a friend. See that you act the part as you should! You understand me, sir. So you shall stay until you've concluded your business in the city. If this is a courtesy, sir, accept it.
PEDANT. Oh, sir, I do — and I shall always regard you as the patron of my life and liberty.

TRANIO. Then come with me, and we'll set the matter up. This, by the way, I should let you understand: my father is expected here any day to pass the bond for a dowry in the marriage between me and one Baptista's daughter here. I'll instruct you in all these circumstances. Come with me to dress as befits you.
[_Exeunt._]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 3 — A room in Petruchio’s house
paragraphs: Enter Katherina and Grumio.
GRUMIO. No, no, truly — I dare not for my life.

KATHERINA. The more I'm wronged, the more his spite shows. What — did he marry me to starve me? Beggars that come to my father's door get an alms on request. If not, they meet charity elsewhere. But I, who never knew how to beg, nor ever needed to, am starved for food, dizzy for lack of sleep — kept awake with oaths and fed with brawling. And what spites me most beyond all these needs — he does it in the name of perfect love, as if to say that if I should sleep or eat, it would be deadly sickness or present death. Please, go and get me something to eat. I don't care what, as long as it's wholesome food.
GRUMIO. What do you say to a calf's foot?
KATHERINA. That's exceedingly good — please let me have it.
GRUMIO. I'm afraid it's too choleric a meat. What do you say to a fat tripe finely grilled?
KATHERINA. I like that well — good Grumio, fetch it for me.
GRUMIO. I can't say — I'm afraid it's choleric. What do you say to a piece of beef and mustard?
KATHERINA. A dish I love to eat.
GRUMIO. Yes, but the mustard is a little too hot.
KATHERINA. Why then, the beef — and let the mustard rest.
GRUMIO. No, then I won't. You shall have the mustard, or else you get no beef from Grumio.
KATHERINA. Then both, or one, or whatever you like.
GRUMIO. Why then, the mustard without the beef.
KATHERINA. Go, get out — you false deluding slave,
[_Beats him._]
you who feed me with just the name of meat. Sorrow upon you and all the pack of you that triumph like this over my misery! Go, get out, I say.
Enter Petruchio with a dish of meat, and Hortensio.
PETRUCHIO. How is my Kate? What, sweetheart — all dejected?
HORTENSIO. Mistress, how are you?
KATHERINA. Honestly — as cold as can be.
PETRUCHIO. Pluck up your spirits. Look at me cheerfully. Here, love — you see how diligent I am, dressing your meat myself and bringing it to you.
[_Sets the dish on a table._]
I'm sure, sweet Kate, this kindness deserves thanks. What — not a word? No, then you don't like it, and all my efforts have come to nothing. Here — take this dish away.
KATHERINA. Please — let it stand.
PETRUCHIO. The smallest service is repaid with thanks. And so shall mine be, before you touch the meat.
KATHERINA. I thank you, sir.
HORTENSIO. Signior Petruchio, for shame — you are to blame. Come, Mistress Kate — I'll keep you company.
PETRUCHIO.
[_Aside._] Eat it all up, Hortensio, if you love me.

Much good may it do your gentle heart! Kate, eat fast. And now, my honey love, we'll return to your father's house and revel there as splendidly as the best, with silken coats and caps and golden rings, with ruffs and cuffs and farthingales and things, with scarves and fans and double change of finery, with amber bracelets, beads, and all this knavery. What — have you dined? The tailor is waiting on your leisure, to deck your body with his ruffling treasure.
Enter Tailor.
Come, tailor, let's see these ornaments. Lay out the gown.
Enter Haberdasher.
What news with you, sir?
HABERDASHER. Here is the cap your worship ordered.
