PETRUCHIO. Why, this was moulded on a porringer — a velvet dish. Fie, fie! It's vulgar and filthy. Why, it's a cockle or a walnut-shell, a knack, a toy, a trick, a baby's cap. Away with it! Come, let me have a bigger one.
KATHERINA. I'll have no bigger. This fits the fashion, and gentlewomen wear caps like these.
PETRUCHIO. When you are gentle, you shall have one too — and not until then.
HORTENSIO.
[_Aside._] That won't be soon.

KATHERINA. Why, sir, I trust I may have leave to speak — and speak I will. I'm no child, no babe. Your betters have allowed me to speak my mind, and if you can't, you'd best stop your ears. My tongue will tell the anger of my heart, or else my heart, holding it in, will break. And rather than have that happen, I'll be free, even to the utmost, to speak as I please.
PETRUCHIO. Why, you speak true — it's a paltry cap, a custard-coffin, a trinket, a silken pie. I love you the more for not liking it.
KATHERINA. Love me or love me not, I like the cap. And this one I'll have, or none at all.
[_Exit Haberdasher._]

PETRUCHIO. Your gown? Why, yes — come, tailor, let's see it. Oh mercy, God! What masquerade stuff is here? What's this? A sleeve? It's like a demi-cannon. What — carved up and down like an apple tart? Here's snip and nip and cut and slish and slash, like a censer in a barber's shop. Why, what in the devil's name, tailor, do you call this?
HORTENSIO.
[_Aside._] I see she's likely to have neither cap nor gown.
TAILOR. You told me to make it orderly and well, according to the fashion and the times.

PETRUCHIO. Indeed, I did — but if you remember, I didn't tell you to ruin it to the times. Go, hop over every gutter on your way home — you'll hop without my custom, sir. I'll have none of it. Off with you! Make the best of it.
KATHERINA. I never saw a better-made gown — more elegant, more pleasing, nor more commendable. It seems you mean to make a puppet of me.
PETRUCHIO. Why, true — he means to make a puppet of you.
TAILOR. She says your worship means to make a puppet of her.

PETRUCHIO. Oh, monstrous arrogance! You lie, you thread, you thimble, you yard, three-quarters, half-yard, quarter, nail! You flea, you nit, you winter-cricket you! Braved in my own house with a skein of thread! Away! You rag, you scrap, you remnant — or I shall so measure you with your own yard-stick that you'll think on prating as long as you live! I tell you — you, you've ruined her gown.
TAILOR. Your worship is mistaken. The gown was made just as my master had directed. Grumio gave the order for how it should be done.
GRUMIO. I gave him no order — I gave him the material.
TAILOR. But how did you want it to be made?
GRUMIO. Indeed, sir, with needle and thread.
TAILOR. But didn't you request it to be cut?
GRUMIO. You've trimmed many things.
TAILOR. I have.

GRUMIO. Don't trim me. You've faced down many men — don't face me. I'll neither be trimmed nor faced. I tell you — I told your master to cut out the gown. But I did not tell him to cut it to pieces. Therefore, you lie.
TAILOR. Why, here's the note of the fashion to testify.
PETRUCHIO. Read it.
GRUMIO. The note lies in his throat, if he says I said so.
TAILOR. '_Imprimis_, a loose-bodied gown.'
GRUMIO. Master, if ever I said 'loose-bodied gown,' sew me in the skirts of it and beat me to death with a ball of brown thread. I said: a gown.
PETRUCHIO. Proceed.
TAILOR. 'With a small compassed cape.'
GRUMIO. I admit the cape.
TAILOR. 'With a trunk sleeve.'
GRUMIO. I admit two sleeves.
TAILOR. 'The sleeves curiously cut.'
PETRUCHIO. Yes — there's the villainy.
GRUMIO. Error in the bill, sir — error in the bill. I ordered that the sleeves should be cut out, and sewn up again. And that I'll prove on you, though your little finger were armed with a thimble.
TAILOR. This is true, what I say — and I had you in a place where you'd know it.
GRUMIO. I'm ready for you straightaway. You take the bill, give me your yard-stick, and don't spare me.
HORTENSIO. God help us, Grumio! Then he shall have no advantage.
PETRUCHIO. Well, sir, in short — the gown is not for me.
GRUMIO. You're right, sir — it's for my mistress.
PETRUCHIO. Go, take it up for your master's use.
GRUMIO. Villain, not for your life! Take up my mistress's gown for your master's use!
PETRUCHIO. Why, sir — what's your meaning in that?
GRUMIO. Oh, sir, the meaning is deeper than you think. Take up my mistress's gown for his master's use! Oh fie, fie, fie!
PETRUCHIO.
[_Aside._] Hortensio, say that you'll see the tailor paid.
[_To Tailor._] Go, take it away — be off, and say no more.
HORTENSIO.
[_Aside to Tailor._] Tailor, I'll pay you for your gown tomorrow.
Don't take offence at his hasty words. Away, I say — give my regards to your master.
[_Exit Tailor._]

PETRUCHIO. Well, come, my Kate — we'll go to your father's, even in these honest plain clothes. Our purses shall be proud, our garments poor — for it's the mind that makes the body rich. And as the sun breaks through the darkest clouds, so honour shows in the poorest dress. Is the jay more precious than the lark because his feathers are more beautiful? Or is the adder better than the eel because his painted skin pleases the eye? Oh no, good Kate — neither are you the worse for this poor furniture and plain array. If you count it a shame, lay it on me. And so be cheerful — we'll go right away to feast and amuse ourselves at your father's house. Go call my men, and let's straight to him. And bring our horses to the end of Long-lane. There we'll mount, and walk to it on foot. Let's see — I think it's now about seven o'clock, and we may well come there by dinner-time.
KATHERINA. I dare assure you, sir, it's nearly two — and it will be supper-time before you arrive.

PETRUCHIO. It shall be seven before I get on the horse. Whatever I say, or do, or think to do — you're still crossing it. Sirs, leave it alone — I won't go today. And before I do, it shall be whatever time of day I say it is.
HORTENSIO. Why, this gallant will command the sun next.
[_Exeunt._]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 4 — Padua. Before Baptista’s house
paragraphs: Enter Tranio and the Pedant dressed like Vincentio.
TRANIO. Sir, this is the house — would you like me to call?
PEDANT. Yes, of course. And unless I'm mistaken, Signior Baptista may remember me from nearly twenty years ago in Genoa, where we were both lodgers at the Pegasus.
TRANIO. That's good. Now hold your own, in any case, with the gravity that befits a father.
PEDANT. I'll guarantee it. But, sir, here comes your boy — he ought to be schooled in his part.
Enter Biondello.
TRANIO. Have no fear about him. Sirrah Biondello, do your duty thoroughly now, I advise you. Imagine he were the real Vincentio.
BIONDELLO. Tut! Don't worry about me.
TRANIO. But have you finished your errand to Baptista?
BIONDELLO. I told him your father was in Venice, and that you expected him in Padua this very day.
TRANIO. You're a fine fellow — here, take this to buy yourself a drink. Here comes Baptista. Compose your face, sir.
Enter Baptista and Lucentio.
Signior Baptista, well met indeed!
[_To the Pedant._] Sir, this is the gentleman I told you of.
I beg you, stand a good father to me now — give me Bianca for my inheritance.

PEDANT. Easy, son! Sir, by your leave: having come to Padua to collect some debts, my son Lucentio informed me of a serious matter — a love between your daughter and himself. And because of the good reputation I hear of you, and because of the love he bears your daughter and she him, I'm content — so as not to delay him too long — as a good father should, to see him matched. And if you're inclined to think no worse of it than I do, then upon some agreement you'll find me ready and willing, with single consent, to have her so bestowed. I cannot be picky with you, Signior Baptista, of whom I hear so much good.

BAPTISTA. Sir, pardon what I'm about to say. Your plainness and brevity please me well. It's quite true that your son Lucentio here loves my daughter, and she loves him — or both of them are deeply concealing their feelings. And so, if you'll say no more than this — that you'll deal with him as a father should, and settle on my daughter a sufficient dowry — the match is made, and everything is decided: your son shall have my daughter with my consent.
TRANIO. Thank you, sir. Now where do you think it best we conclude the betrothal, and have such assurances exchanged as will satisfy both parties?
BAPTISTA. Not in my house, Lucentio — you know that pitchers have ears, and I have many servants. Besides, old Gremio is always listening, and we could easily be interrupted.

TRANIO. Then at my lodging, if it suits you. My father is staying there, and there tonight we'll handle the business privately and well. Send for your daughter by your servant here. My boy will fetch the scrivener at once. The worst part is that, on such short notice, you're likely to have only a thin and meager supper.

BAPTISTA. That suits me well. Cambio, hurry home and tell Bianca to make herself ready right away. And, if you like, tell her what's happened: Lucentio's father has arrived in Padua, and she's likely to become Lucentio's wife.
LUCENTIO. I pray the gods she may — with all my heart!
TRANIO. Don't waste time on the gods — get going. Signior Baptista, shall I lead the way? Welcome! One simple course is likely to be your fare. Come, sir — we'll make it up to you in Pisa.
BAPTISTA. I'll follow you.
[_Exeunt Tranio, Pedant and Baptista._]
BIONDELLO. Cambio!
LUCENTIO. What are you saying, Biondello?
BIONDELLO. Did you see my master wink and laugh at you?
LUCENTIO. Biondello, what about it?
BIONDELLO. Faith, nothing — except he's left me here behind to explain the meaning or moral of his signs and signals.
LUCENTIO. Please, then, interpret them for me.
BIONDELLO. Like this, then: Baptista is safe, busy talking with the false father of a deceitful son.
LUCENTIO. And what of him?
BIONDELLO. His daughter is to be brought by you to the supper.
LUCENTIO. And then?
BIONDELLO. The old priest at Saint Luke's church is at your command at any hour.
LUCENTIO. And what does all this mean?

BIONDELLO. I can't say for certain — except that they're busy with a counterfeit betrothal. Take your assurance of her, _cum privilegio ad imprimendum solum_ — to the church! Take the priest, clerk, and some sufficient honest witnesses. If this isn't what you're looking for, I've nothing more to say, except — bid Bianca farewell for ever and a day.
[_Going._]
LUCENTIO. Do you hear me, Biondello?

BIONDELLO. I can't linger. I once knew a girl who was married in an afternoon, while she was going into the garden for parsley to stuff a rabbit — and so it may be with you, sir. So farewell, sir. My master has ordered me to go to Saint Luke's and tell the priest to be ready when you arrive with your appendix.
[_Exit._]
LUCENTIO. I may, and will, if she's willing. She'll be pleased — so why should I doubt? Come what may, I'll go straight to her. It would be a hard thing if Cambio went without her.
[_Exit._]

chapters.title: Act 4, Scene 5 — A public road
paragraphs: Enter Petruchio, Katherina, Hortensio and Servants.
PETRUCHIO. Come on, in God's name — once more toward our father's house. Good Lord, how bright and lovely the moon shines!
KATHERINA. The moon! It's the sun — it is not moonlight now.
PETRUCHIO. I say it's the moon that shines so brightly.
KATHERINA. I know it's the sun that shines so brightly.

PETRUCHIO. Now by my mother's son — and that's myself — it shall be moon, or star, or whatever I please, before I travel another step toward your father's house. Go on and fetch our horses back again. Always crossed and crossed — nothing but crossed!
HORTENSIO. Say what he says, or we'll never go.
KATHERINA. Forward, please, since we've come so far. And let it be moon, or sun, or whatever you please. And if you please to call it a rush-candle, from now on I vow it shall be so for me.
PETRUCHIO. I say it is the moon.
KATHERINA. I know it is the moon.
PETRUCHIO. No, then you lie — it's the blessed sun.

KATHERINA. Then, God be blessed, it is the blessed sun. But it is not the sun when you say it is not, and the moon changes just as your mind does. Whatever you wish it to be called, that is what it is — and so it shall be for Katherine.
HORTENSIO. Petruchio, carry on — the battle is won.
PETRUCHIO. Well, forward, forward! That's how the bowl should run, and not unluckily against the bias. But, soft! Company is coming this way.
Enter Vincentio, in travelling dress.
[_To Vincentio._] Good morning, gentle mistress — where are you going?

Tell me, sweet Kate, and tell me truly — have you ever seen a fresher young woman? Such a war of white and red in her cheeks! What stars adorn the heavens with such beauty as those two eyes that grace that heavenly face? Fair lovely maid, once more good day to you. Sweet Kate, embrace her for her beauty's sake.
HORTENSIO. He'll make the man mad, turning him into a woman.

KATHERINA. Young budding virgin, fair and fresh and sweet — where are you going, or where is your home? Happy are the parents of so fair a child. Happier still the man whom favorable stars assign you to be his lovely bedfellow.
PETRUCHIO. Why, how now, Kate! I hope you're not mad: this is a man — old, wrinkled, faded, withered — and not a maiden, as you say he is.

KATHERINA. Pardon me, old father, for my mistaking eyes — they've been so dazzled by the sun that everything I look at seems green. Now I see you're a reverend father. Pardon me, I pray you, for my foolish mistake.
PETRUCHIO. Do, good old grandsire — and also tell us which way you're travelling. If it's along with us, we'll be glad of your company.

VINCENTIO. Fair sir, and you my merry mistress — who much amazed me with your strange encounter — my name is Vincentio. My home is Pisa, and I'm bound for Padua to visit a son of mine whom I haven't seen in a long while.
PETRUCHIO. What is his name?
VINCENTIO. Lucentio, gentle sir.

PETRUCHIO. Well met — and even better met for your son's sake. And now, by law as well as by your venerable age, I may rightfully call you my loving father: this gentlewoman, sister to my wife, your son has by now married. Don't be astonished, and don't be grieved — she is of good standing, her dowry generous, and her birth worthy. Besides, she is so qualified as to befit the wife of any noble gentleman. Let me embrace old Vincentio — and let us go together to see your honest son, who will be overjoyed at your arrival.
VINCENTIO. But is this true? Or is it simply your pleasure, like jolly travellers, to play a joke on the company you've overtaken?
HORTENSIO. I assure you, father, it is so.
PETRUCHIO. Come, come along, and see the truth of it for yourself — our first piece of fun has made you suspicious.
[_Exeunt all but Hortensio._]
HORTENSIO. Well, Petruchio, this has put fresh heart into me. Off to my widow! And if she's contrary, then you've taught Hortensio how to be just as contrary in return.
[_Exit._]

chapters.title: Act 5, Scene 1 — Padua. Before Lucentio’s house
paragraphs: Enter on one side Biondello, Lucentio and Bianca; Gremio walking on the other side.
BIONDELLO. Softly and swiftly, sir — the priest is ready.
LUCENTIO. I'll fly, Biondello — but they may need you at home, so leave us.
BIONDELLO. No, truly, I'll see you safely into the church and back, and then return to my master's as soon as I can.
[_Exeunt Lucentio, Bianca and Biondello._]
GREMIO. I'm amazed Cambio hasn't come all this while.
Enter Petruchio, Katherina, Vincentio and Attendants.
PETRUCHIO. Sir, here's the door — this is Lucentio's house. My father's lies more toward the marketplace; that's where I must go, and so here I leave you, sir.
VINCENTIO. You shan't go without drinking with us first. I think I can secure your welcome here, and by all likelihood some good cheer is on the way.
[_Knocks._]
GREMIO. They're busy inside — you'd best knock louder.
Enter Pedant above, at a window.
PEDANT. Who is it that knocks as if he'd beat down the gate?
VINCENTIO. Is Signior Lucentio inside, sir?
PEDANT. He's inside, sir, but not to be spoken to.
VINCENTIO. What if a man brought him a hundred pound or two to make merry with?
PEDANT. Keep your hundred pounds to yourself — he'll need none as long as I live.

PETRUCHIO. No, I told you your son was well loved in Padua. Do you hear, sir? To set frivolous matters aside, please tell Signior Lucentio that his father has come from Pisa, and is here at the door to speak with him.
PEDANT. You lie — his father has come from Padua, and is here looking out the window.
VINCENTIO. Are you his father?
PEDANT. Yes, sir — so his mother says, if I may believe her.
PETRUCHIO.
[_To Vincentio._] Why, how now, gentleman! This is plain knavery — to
take on you another man's name.
PEDANT. Lay hands on the villain — I believe he means to cheat someone in this city under cover of my identity.
Re-enter Biondello.
BIONDELLO. I've seen them in the church together — God send them good sailing! But who is here? My old master, Vincentio! Now we are undone and brought to nothing.
VINCENTIO.
[_Seeing Biondello._] Come here, gallows-bird.
BIONDELLO. I hope I have a choice, sir.
VINCENTIO. Come here, you rogue. What — have you forgotten me?
BIONDELLO. Forgotten you! No, sir — I couldn't have forgotten you, for I've never seen you before in my life.
VINCENTIO. What, you notorious villain! Have you never seen your master's father, Vincentio?
BIONDELLO. What, my old worshipful master? Yes indeed, sir — look where he's looking out of the window.
VINCENTIO. Is that so, really?
[_He beats Biondello._]
BIONDELLO. Help, help, help! Here's a madman who'll murder me.
[_Exit._]
PEDANT. Help, son! Help, Signior Baptista!
[_Exit from the window._]
PETRUCHIO. Please, Kate, let's stand aside and see how this quarrel ends.
[_They retire._]
Re-enter Pedant, below; Baptista, Tranio and Servants.
TRANIO. Sir, who are you to dare to beat my servant?

VINCENTIO. Who am I, sir! No — who are you, sir? O immortal gods! O fine villain! A silken doublet, velvet hose, a scarlet cloak, and a sugar-loaf hat! O, I'm ruined! I'm ruined! While I play the thrifty householder at home, my son and my servant spend everything at the university.
TRANIO. How now! What's the matter?
BAPTISTA. What — is the man a lunatic?

TRANIO. Sir, you seem a sober elderly gentleman by your dress, but your words mark you as a madman. Why, sir, what concern is it of yours if I wear pearl and gold? I thank my good father — I am able to maintain it.
VINCENTIO. Your father! O villain! He's a sailmaker in Bergamo.
BAPTISTA. You're mistaken, sir — you're mistaken. Pray, what do you think is his name?
VINCENTIO. His name! As if I didn't know his name! I've brought him up ever since he was three years old, and his name is Tranio.
PEDANT. Away, away, mad ass! His name is Lucentio — and he is my only son, and heir to my lands, I, Signior Vincentio.
VINCENTIO. Lucentio! O, he's murdered his master! Lay hold of him, I charge you, in the Duke's name. O, my son, my son! Tell me, you villain — where is my son Lucentio?
TRANIO. Call an officer.
Enter one with an Officer.
Take this mad rogue to the jail. Father Baptista, I charge you to see that he be produced when required.
VINCENTIO. Take me to the jail!
GREMIO. Wait, officer — he shall not go to prison.
BAPTISTA. Hold your tongue, Signior Gremio — I say he shall go to prison.
GREMIO. Take care, Signior Baptista, lest you be taken in by this scheme. I dare swear this is the real Vincentio.
PEDANT. Swear it, if you dare.
GREMIO. No, I dare not swear it.
TRANIO. Then you'd best say I'm not Lucentio.
GREMIO. Yes, I know you to be Signior Lucentio.
BAPTISTA. Away with the old fool! To the jail with him!
VINCENTIO. So strangers may be hauled about and abused — O monstrous villain!
Re-enter Biondello, with Lucentio and Bianca.
BIONDELLO. O! We're done for — and there he is. Deny him, disown him, or else we're all undone.
LUCENTIO.
[_Kneeling._] Pardon, sweet father.
VINCENTIO. Does my sweetest son still live?
[_Biondello, Tranio and Pedant run out._]
BIANCA.
[_Kneeling._] Pardon, dear father.
BAPTISTA. How have you offended? Where is Lucentio?
LUCENTIO. Here is Lucentio — true son of the true Vincentio — who has by marriage made your daughter mine, while counterfeit pretenses blinded your eyes.
GREMIO. Here's a plot indeed — proof positive of how we've all been deceived!
VINCENTIO. Where is that damned villain Tranio, who faced and defied me in this matter so brazenly?
BAPTISTA. Why, tell me — is this not my Cambio?
BIANCA. Cambio is changed into Lucentio.

LUCENTIO. Love worked these miracles. Bianca's love made me exchange my position with Tranio, while he took on my appearance in town. And happily I have at last arrived at the longed-for haven of my bliss. What Tranio did, I forced him to do — so pardon him, sweet father, for my sake.
VINCENTIO. I'll slit the villain's nose — the one who would have sent me to jail!
BAPTISTA.
[_To Lucentio._] But do you hear, sir? Have you married my daughter
without asking my consent?
VINCENTIO. Don't worry, Baptista — we'll satisfy you, never fear. But I'll go inside, to take revenge for this villainy.
[_Exit._]
BAPTISTA. And I'll go in to sound the depth of this knavery.
[_Exit._]
LUCENTIO. Don't look pale, Bianca — your father won't frown.
[_Exeunt Lucentio and Bianca._]
GREMIO. My cake is dough — but I'll go in with the rest, having lost all hope of anything but my share of the feast.
[_Exit._]
Petruchio and Katherina come forward.
KATHERINA. Husband, let's follow them to see the end of this commotion.
PETRUCHIO. First kiss me, Kate, and then we will.
KATHERINA. What! In the middle of the street?
PETRUCHIO. What! Are you ashamed of me?
KATHERINA. No, sir — God forbid; but ashamed to kiss in public.
PETRUCHIO. Why, then, let's go home again. Come, sirrah, let's away.
KATHERINA. No, I will give you a kiss. Now please, love, stay.
PETRUCHIO. Isn't this good? Come, my sweet Kate. Better once than never — for never is too late.
[_Exeunt._]

chapters.title: Act 5, Scene 2 — A room in Lucentio’s house
paragraphs: Enter Baptista, Vincentio, Gremio, the Pedant, Lucentio, Bianca, Petruchio, Katherina, Hortensio and Widow. Tranio, Biondello, Grumio and Others, attending.

LUCENTIO. At last — though long in coming — our jarring notes agree. And it is time, when raging war is done, to smile at narrow escapes and dangers past. My fair Bianca, bid my father welcome, while I with the same kindness welcome yours. Brother Petruchio, sister Katherina, and you, Hortensio, with your loving widow — feast with the best, and welcome to my house. My banquet is to settle our stomachs after our great good cheer. Please, sit down — for now we sit to chat as well as to eat.
[_They sit at table._]
PETRUCHIO. Nothing but sit and sit, and eat and eat!
BAPTISTA. Padua offers this kindness, son Petruchio.
PETRUCHIO. Padua offers nothing that is not kind.
HORTENSIO. For both our sakes, I wish that word were true.
PETRUCHIO. Now, on my life, Hortensio is afraid of his widow.
WIDOW. Then never trust me, if I am afraid.
PETRUCHIO. You're very quick, and yet you miss my meaning: I mean Hortensio is afraid of you.
WIDOW. He who is dizzy thinks the world turns round.
PETRUCHIO. Roundly replied.
KATHERINA. Mistress, what do you mean by that?
WIDOW. This is what I gather from him.
PETRUCHIO. Conceives from me! How does Hortensio like that?
HORTENSIO. My widow says this is how she conceives her meaning.
PETRUCHIO. Very well patched. Kiss him for that, good widow.
KATHERINA. 'He who is dizzy thinks the world turns round' — please tell me what you meant by that.
WIDOW. Your husband, being troubled with a shrew, measures my husband's sorrow by his own woe. And now you know my meaning.
KATHERINA. A very mean meaning.
WIDOW. Right — I mean you.
KATHERINA. And I am mean, indeed, by comparison with you.
PETRUCHIO. At her, Kate!
HORTENSIO. At her, widow!
PETRUCHIO. A hundred marks, my Kate puts her down.
HORTENSIO. That's my office.
PETRUCHIO. Spoken like an officer — here's to you, lad.
[_Drinks to Hortensio._]
BAPTISTA. How does Gremio like these quick-witted folk?
GREMIO. Believe me, sir, they butt heads well together.
BIANCA. Head and butt! A hasty-witted person would say your head and butt were head and horn.
VINCENTIO. Aye, mistress bride — has that woken you up?
BIANCA. Aye, but it hasn't frightened me — therefore I'll sleep again.
PETRUCHIO. No, you shan't. Since you've begun, prepare for a sharp jest or two.
BIANCA. Am I your bird? I mean to change my bush — then pursue me as you draw your bow. You are welcome, all of you.
[_Exeunt Bianca, Katherina and Widow._]
PETRUCHIO. She's gotten ahead of me. Here, Signior Tranio — this is the bird you aimed at, though you didn't hit her. So a toast to all who shot and missed.
TRANIO. O, sir! Lucentio slipped me like his greyhound, who runs by himself and catches for his master.
PETRUCHIO. A good swift simile — but somewhat doggish.
TRANIO. It's just as well, sir, that you hunted for yourself — it's thought your deer holds you at bay.
BAPTISTA. O ho, Petruchio! Tranio hits you now.
LUCENTIO. I thank you for that thrust, good Tranio.
HORTENSIO. Confess, confess — hasn't he hit you here?
PETRUCHIO. He's chafed me a little, I admit. And as the jest glanced off me, it's ten to one it wounded you two outright.
BAPTISTA. Now, in good earnest, son Petruchio, I think you have the most genuine shrew of all.

PETRUCHIO. Well, I say no — and therefore, for proof, let each of us send for his wife. And the one whose wife is most obedient — who comes first when he sends for her — shall win the wager we'll propose.
HORTENSIO. Agreed. What's the wager?
LUCENTIO. Twenty crowns.
PETRUCHIO. Twenty crowns! I'd venture that much on my hawk or hound — but twenty times that much on my wife.
LUCENTIO. A hundred, then.
HORTENSIO. Agreed.
PETRUCHIO. A match! It's done.
HORTENSIO. Who shall begin?
LUCENTIO. I will. Go, Biondello — tell your mistress to come to me.
BIONDELLO. I go.
[_Exit._]
BAPTISTA. Son, I'll go halves with you that Bianca will come.
LUCENTIO. I'll have no halves — I'll bear it all myself.
Re-enter Biondello.
How now! What news?
BIONDELLO. Sir, my mistress sends word that she is busy and cannot come.
PETRUCHIO. What! She's busy, and she cannot come! Is that an answer?
GREMIO. Aye, and a kind one too — pray God, sir, your wife send you no worse.
PETRUCHIO. I hope better.
HORTENSIO. Sirrah Biondello, go and entreat my wife to come to me at once.
[_Exit Biondello._]
PETRUCHIO. O, ho! Entreat her! No — then she must come.
HORTENSIO. I'm afraid, sir, that whatever you may do, yours will not be entreated.
Re-enter Biondello.
Now, where is my wife?
BIONDELLO. She says you have some fine jest in hand. She will not come — she bids you come to her.
PETRUCHIO. Worse and worse — she will not come! O vile, intolerable, not to be endured! Sirrah Grumio, go to your mistress — say I command her to come to me.
[_Exit Grumio._]
HORTENSIO. I know her answer.
PETRUCHIO. What?
HORTENSIO. She will not.
PETRUCHIO. The worse luck for me — and there's an end.
Re-enter Katherina.
BAPTISTA. Now, by my faith — here comes Katherina!
KATHERINA. What is your will, sir, that you send for me?
PETRUCHIO. Where is your sister, and Hortensio's wife?
KATHERINA. They are sitting and talking by the parlour fire.
PETRUCHIO. Go fetch them here. If they refuse to come, beat them soundly out to their husbands. Away, I say, and bring them here at once.
[_Exit Katherina._]
LUCENTIO. Here's a wonder, if you talk of wonders.
HORTENSIO. And so it is. I wonder what it foretells.
PETRUCHIO. Indeed, it foretells peace — and love, and quiet life, awe-inspiring rule, and rightful authority. And, in short, everything that is sweet and happy.

BAPTISTA. Now, good fortune to you, good Petruchio! You have won the wager — and I'll add to their losses twenty thousand crowns: another dowry to another daughter, for she is changed, as if she had never been the same.

PETRUCHIO. No, I'll win my wager better still, and show more proof of her obedience — her newly built virtue and obedience. See where she comes, bringing your contrary wives as prisoners to her womanly persuasion.
Re-enter Katherina with Bianca and Widow.
Katherine, that cap of yours doesn't suit you. Off with that bauble — throw it underfoot.
[_Katherina pulls off her cap and throws it down._]
WIDOW. Lord, may I never have cause to sigh till I'm reduced to such a silly state!
BIANCA. Fie! What a foolish duty do you call this?
LUCENTIO. I wish your duty were as foolish too. The wisdom of your duty, fair Bianca, has cost me a hundred crowns since suppertime!
BIANCA. The more fool you, for wagering on my duty.
PETRUCHIO. Katherine, I charge you — tell these headstrong women what duty they owe their lords and husbands.
WIDOW. Come, come, you're mocking — we'll have no lecturing.
PETRUCHIO. Come on, I say — and begin first with her.
WIDOW. She shall not.
PETRUCHIO. I say she shall — and begin first with her.

KATHERINA. Fie, fie! Unknit that threatening, unkind brow, and don't dart scornful glances from those eyes to wound your lord, your king, your governor. It blots your beauty as frost bites the meadows, ruins your reputation as whirlwinds shake fair buds — and in no way is it fitting or amiable. A woman moved is like a troubled fountain: muddy, ugly, thick, stripped of beauty. And while it is so, no one — however dry or thirsty — will deign to sip or touch a drop of it. Your husband is your lord, your life, your keeper, your head, your sovereign — one who cares for you, and for your maintenance commits his body to painful labour both by sea and land, to keep watch by night in storms, by day in cold, while you lie warm at home, secure and safe. And he asks no other tribute from you but love, kind looks, and true obedience — too small a payment for so great a debt. The same duty a subject owes the prince, a woman owes her husband. And when she is contrary, peevish, sullen, sour, and not obedient to his honest will, what is she but a foul, contentious rebel, and an ungrateful traitor to her loving lord? I am ashamed that women are so simple as to offer war where they should kneel for peace, or seek rule, supremacy, and command, when they are bound to serve, love, and obey. Why are our bodies soft and weak and smooth, unfit for toil and trouble in the world, except that our gentle natures and our hearts should match our outward form? Come, come, you contrary and incapable creatures! My spirit has been as big as any of yours, my heart as great, my reason perhaps more — to trade word for word and frown for frown. But now I see our lances are only straws, our strength as weak, our weakness beyond compare — seeming most what we are in truth the least. Then lower your prides, for it's no use, and place your hands beneath your husband's foot. As a token of that duty, if he please, my hand is ready — may it bring him ease.
PETRUCHIO. Why, there's a woman! Come on, and kiss me, Kate.
LUCENTIO. Well, carry on, old lad — for you've won it.
VINCENTIO. It's a fine thing to hear, when children are dutiful.
LUCENTIO. But a harsh thing to hear, when women are contrary.
PETRUCHIO. Come, Kate, let's go to bed. We three are married — but you two are bested. It was I who won the wager,
[_To Lucentio._] though you hit the bullseye —
and being a winner, God give you good night!
[_Exeunt Petruchio and Katherina._]
HORTENSIO. Now go your ways — you've tamed a cursed shrew.
LUCENTIO. It's a wonder, by your leave, that she will be tamed so.
[_Exeunt._]
